Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Juzayy mentionnent aussi ces divergences. Ibn Kathir cite le hadith de Khaybar comme illustration de l'attaque surprise, qu'al-Zamakhshari présente comme une image. Ibn Ashur voit dans le second « temps » une référence possible à la fin de la vie du Prophète ou à l'au-delà. Les commentateurs ne tranchent pas entre ces lectures, qui convergent toutes vers l'affermissement du Prophète et l'avertissement aux incrédules.

Le verset conclut la sourate par la glorification de Dieu, exalté au-dessus des attributs que lui prêtent les associateurs, à savoir la progéniture et les associés. Le sens premier est : gloire à ton Seigneur, ô Muhammad, Maître de la puissance et de la force, au-dessus de ce qu'ils décrivent. Les commentateurs s'accordent à adresser le discours au Prophète ﷺ et à entendre par « al-‘izza » la force et la victoire. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir expliquent que le tasbih signifie la purification de Dieu de tout ce qui ne Lui convient pas, Qatada précisant qu'il s'agit de mensonges. Al-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan disent que le Seigneur est dit maître de la puissance parce qu'il en a l'exclusivité, tandis qu'al-Nasafi et d'autres ajoutent qu'il est maître de toute puissance dont jouissent les créatures. Pour la formule « Paix sur les envoyés », Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi y voient la sauvegarde des envoyés de ce qu'on a dit de Dieu, et al-Mawardi propose deux lectures : un honneur qui leur est rendu ou la protection contre la mort. Enfin « Louange à Dieu, Seigneur des mondes » est compris par al-Tabari comme la louange exclusive pour les bienfaits, et par Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Kathir comme la louange pour la destruction des ennemis et le secours des prophètes, tandis qu'al-Shawkani et Abu al-Su'ud y voient une louange générale pour toutes les grâces. Plusieurs commentateurs rapportent des traditions sur le mérite de réciter ces versets à la fin de la prière ou d'une assemblée ; Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi en soulignent la faiblesse, et aucun ne tranche entre les avis.

Dieu clôt la sourate as-Saffat en se purifiant de ce que lui attribuent les païens, fils et associés, car il est le Seigneur de la puissance et de la gloire. Il adresse ensuite son salut aux envoyés, c'est-à-dire qu'il proclame leur sécurité et leur paix face à ce qu'ils ont dit de leur Seigneur et aux épreuves subies de la part de leurs peuples. Puis il loue Dieu pour les bienfaits accordés à ses serviteurs et pour la victoire donnée à ses prophètes. Les commentateurs expliquent que le salut signifie ici l'honneur et la salutation, mais aussi l'annonce de leur sauvegarde contre les épreuves et de leur sécurité au jour de la grande frayeur. Par « les envoyés », ils entendent les prophètes qui transmettent l'unicité divine et les lois révélées, certains y incluant les anges chargés d'exécuter les ordres divins. Ils s'accordent à dire que ce que les envoyés ont affirmé de leur Seigneur est exempt de tout défaut, ce qui motive ce salut. Al-Shawkani et Ibn Ashur voient dans ce verset une conclusion qui résume les thèmes de la sourate : purification de Dieu, éloge des envoyés et louange pour les grâces accordées. Ibn al-Qayyim explique que le salut est ici une demande ou une invocation, qu'il peut émaner de Dieu sous forme d'engagement envers lui-même. Des traditions rapportées par Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Anas et d'autres indiquent que le Prophète récitait ce passage à la fin de sa prière ou de son assemblée, et que celui qui le fait en quittant une assemblée obtient une récompense abondante, bien que la plupart des critiques de hadith fragilisent ces chaînes de transmission. Les commentateurs ne tirent du verset aucune règle juridique précise, sinon la recommandation de le réciter à la clôture d'une réunion.

Ce verset clôt la sourate as-Saffat par une glorification de Dieu, qui se déclare exempt de ce que les infidèles lui attribuent, enfants ou associés. Il est le Seigneur de la puissance, qui élève qui il veut et abaisse qui il veut. Dieu salue ensuite les messagers, car tout ce qu'ils ont dit de leur Seigneur est exempt de défaut, puis il se loue lui-même pour ses bienfaits, pour l'envoi des prophètes et pour la victoire de ceux-ci sur leurs ennemis. Les commentateurs considèrent ce passage comme une conclusion qui résume les thèmes de la sourate : la réfutation des croyances polythéistes et l'affermissement des prophètes.

Les commentateurs s'accordent pour dire que la louange revêt plusieurs sens : louer Dieu pour l'envoi des messagers comme annonciateurs et avertisseurs, ou pour l'ensemble de ses bienfaits envers les créatures, selon al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi et Ibn Kathir. Al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir y voient plutôt la louange pour la perte des ennemis et la victoire des prophètes, tandis qu'al-Qurtubi juge que tous ces sens sont visés à la fois. Ibn Kathir relie la glorification à la négation de tout défaut et la louange à l'affirmation de la perfection.

Sur le sens de « Seigneur de la puissance », al-Mawardi donne deux lectures, « maître de la puissance » ou « Seigneur de tout ce qui se dit puissant » ; al-Zamakhshari y voit une annexion d'exclusivité, et Ibn 'Atiyya estime qu'il s'agit de la puissance créée qu'accordent les hommes. Quant au salut sur les messagers, al-Mawardi le lit comme un honneur qui leur est rendu ou comme l'annonce de leur sauvegarde. Al-Tabari rapporte, d'après Qatada, un hadith sur le salut adressé aux messagers.

Plusieurs récits rapportent que réciter ces versets en fin d'assemblée ou après la prière procure une grande récompense, mais Ibn Kathir et d'autres signalent la faiblesse de leurs chaînes de transmission, de sorte que ces transmissions ne sont pas tenues pour établies.
en: God swears at the opening of Surat al-Saffat by several groups of angels. The ones who line up in rows are, according to Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, Qatada, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the angels arrayed in the heavens or with their wings spread in the air awaiting God's command; al-Tabari judges this the most convincing reading. Those who drive away with force are, for al-Suddi, the angels who drive the clouds, while Qatada takes them to be the verses of the Quran that restrain from wrongdoing. Those who recite the Reminder are the angels who recite God's Book, according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and others, or, according to Mawardi, the prophets reciting the remembrance to their peoples. The oath is answered by the statement that your God is one. It is followed by the explanation that He is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and what lies between them, and the Lord of the easts. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the sun has three hundred and sixty risings, matching the days of the year, and that mentioning the easts makes the wests understood. The passage then describes the adorning of the lowest heaven with stars and its protection from rebellious devils, who cannot listen to the exalted assembly; whoever snatches a word is pursued by a piercing flame. On recitation, Abu 'Amr and Hamza assimilate the ta' into the sad, zay and dhal, a reading that al-Nahhas considers weak from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, while Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi point to the closeness of these sounds and the others read it with the sounds kept distinct.

At the opening of Surat al-Saffat God swears by groups of angels: by those who stand in ranks, by those who drive forcefully, and by those who recite the reminder. Most commentators, including Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, take these terms to refer to angels. The 'ranks' are the angels arrayed in the heavens, or their wings spread in the air awaiting God's command; the 'drivers' are the angels who drive the clouds; the 'reciters' are the angels who recite God's words. Al-Tabari adopts this reading as the most convincing, since God begins with a category of angels all agree on, namely the ranked ones. Other scholars read the terms differently: Qatada took the 'drivers' to be the Quranic verses that forbid evil and the 'reciters' to be people who recite the Book; al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari allowed that the ranks may be worshippers or fighters standing in lines, and the reciters may be scholars or prophets. The particle fa linking the three terms is read by some as expressing a sequence of occurrence and by others as a ranking of merit. The oath's answer is that your God is one, Lord of the heavens, the earth, what lies between them and the risings of the sun. The readers differ too: Abu 'Amr and Hamza assimilate the ta into the following letter, while the rest pronounce it clearly.

At the opening of Surat as-Saffat God swears by groups of angels: those who stand in ranks, those who drive away, and those who recite the reminder, and then He states what the oath is for, namely that your God is one. Most commentators understand the three descriptions as referring to angels. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain that the ranks are the rows of angels in heaven, some adding that they spread their wings in the air awaiting God's command, while al-Hasan takes them as the rows of angels before their Lord in prayer. For the drivers, as-Suddi and Mujahid say they are the angels who drive the clouds, while az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand them as those who restrain from sin through admonition, and Qatada as the verses of the Qur'an that forbid wrongdoing. As for the reciters, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid and as-Suddi identify them as the angels who recite God's scriptures, Qatada as the people who recite the Book, and al-Mawardi as the prophets. Ibn Kathir and ash-Shawkani judge the first view, that they are angels, to be the preferable one. Some exegetes note that the particle fa linking the descriptions indicates an order, whether of excellence or of sequence. The purpose of the oath is to affirm God's oneness: He is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and what lies between them, and the Lord of the risings. The commentators add that the stars adorn the nearest heaven and guard it against rebellious devils, who are struck by shooting stars when they try to eavesdrop on the higher assembly.

In this opening, God swears by the angels in their ranks, by those who drive away, and by those who recite His remembrance, and then states what the oath affirms: your God is one. The commentators explain that the verse means that the God of humanity is one, the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, and the Lord of the easts, that is the points where the sun rises through the year; whoever creates and governs the universe in this way alone deserves worship. They note that the wording is general and can cover angels arranged in prayer or with wings spread in the air, those who drive the clouds or turn people from sin, and those who recite God's words or remember Him.

Most exegetes, including Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir, take these three descriptions to refer to the angels. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi accept that they may also cover birds, believers standing in rows in prayer or battle, the verses of the Qur'an, or prophets reciting the message to their peoples. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the particle fa linking these attributes indicates either an order of merit or an order among the things described. As for the easts, al-Suddi and al-Qurtubi count three hundred and sixty, the number of days in the year, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi also allow that the reference may be to the risings of stars, and that only the easts are mentioned because sunrise comes before sunset. Al-Tabari adds that mentioning God as Lord of the easts points to the evidence of His power.

Readers differ on some recitation points, such as the assimilation of the ta in al-Saffat, which Ibn Hanbal disliked according to al-Shawkani, and on the readings of zinatin and al-kawakib; al-Tabari prefers the reading with the genitive construction.

At the opening of Surat al-Saffat, God swears by groups of angels who stand in rows in worship, drive away the clouds, and recite the remembrance, and then declares that your God is one. Verse 5 establishes this oneness through the attribute of Lord: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and the Lord of the easts. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the meaning is that He is the creator, owner and governor of everything between heaven and earth, and worship belongs only to the one who has these attributes. The commentators agree that the easts are the risings of the sun, which rises each day from a different point; mentioning the easts suffices to imply the wests, as Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Jawzi note. As-Suddi reports their number as three hundred and sixty, while Yahya ibn Salam counts one hundred and eighty; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi reconcile the two figures by different ways of counting. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the dual forms in Surat ar-Rahman refer to the easts of summer and winter, while the singular refers to the direction. Commentators also observe that the Lord of the heavens and the earth serves as proof of divine unity: the one who governs so vast an order cannot have a partner, as Ibn Sa'di and Abu al-Su'ud point out.

This verse states that God adorned the nearest heaven, the lower sky, with an adornment: the shining stars. The commentators read it as a sign of the Creator's greatness and wisdom, since the stars beautify the sky and guide travellers on land and sea. The readers differ on the wording: most read "bi-zinati al-kawakib" with the noun in construct, while Hamza and Hafs read "bi-zinatin al-kawakibi" with tanwin and the stars in the genitive as an apposition, and Abu Bakr reads "al-kawakiba" in the accusative. Al-Tabari judges the construct reading the most sound, and reports that Ibn Abbas understood the adornment as the light of the stars. Ibn Kathir explains that the planets and fixed stars illuminate the transparent expanse of the sky. Al-Razi lists several aspects of this beauty: the brightness, the varied shapes of the constellations, and their appearance to viewers below. All agree that the stars also serve as a guard, protecting the heaven from rebellious devils who tried to eavesdrop on the angels, and that these devils are struck by shooting stars. The scholars differ on when this began: al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that it intensified with the Prophet's mission, while others hold that it existed before. Some note that the shooting star burns or afflicts the devil without necessarily killing him. The commentators report these views without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that God adorned the nearest heaven with shining stars and made them a guard against rebellious devils, so that they cannot eavesdrop on the highest assembly, that is, the angels. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that devils once ascended to heaven, snatched a word of revelation or decree, and passed it to their human allies among the soothsayers, who added a hundred lies to it, and that this changed with the prophetic mission, so that a shooting flame now pursues anyone attempting such stealth. All agree that the word 'marid' means one who is rebellious, stripped of good, and that 'dhuhur' means expulsion and banishment, while the lasting punishment is understood as either perpetual or painful. On the reading 'yassammaʿun' with doubling, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as 'they seek to listen', and al-Tabari prefers the single-letter reading on the basis of the reports. Ibn Abbas holds that the shooting flame does not kill but burns or disables, while others take it as a bright star; al-Razi distinguishes these shooting lights from the fixed stars, and al-Zamakhshari shows that 'zinah' may be a verbal noun or a name depending on the reading. The grammatical role of 'hifzan' is debated, but the commentators agree that the core meaning is unaffected.

This passage from Surat as-Saffat states that the devils cannot listen to the highest assembly, meaning the angels in the heavens, and that they are pelted with meteors from every side as a rejection, with a lasting punishment. The commentators agree that the heavens were guarded against eavesdroppers. They differ on how to read the verb yassammaʿūna. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean that the devils try to listen but do not succeed, while al-Tabari prefers the lighter reading, relying on reports that devils used to overhear revelation until they were struck by shooting stars. Abu Ubayd preferred the doubled form, since the Arabs say tasammaʿa ilayhi rather than samiʿa ilayhi. On al-mala al-aʿlā, Qatada identifies it with the lowest heaven, as-Suddi with the angels, and Ibn Abbas with the scribes or the noblest angels. On wāsib, Mujahid and Qatada say it means lasting, as-Suddi and Abu Salih say painful, and al-Tabari chooses the sense of enduring and pure. Ibn Abbas holds that the meteor burns the devil without killing him, leaving him disabled. Al-Qurtubi links the intensified guarding to the mission of the Prophet. Az-Zamakhshari treats the clause as an independent narrative, while others take it as a description or a cause of the protection, readings that the grammarians found weak.

The verse « duhuran wa lahum 'adhabun wasib » describes the demons who try to eavesdrop on the heavens: they are pelted with shooting stars from every side, driven away from the exalted assembly of the angels, and a lasting punishment awaits them. The commentators agree that duhur means being repelled and driven away. As for wasib, al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, Ikrima and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean lasting, while al-Sudi, Abu Salih and al-Kalbi take it to mean painful, reaching the heart. Al-Tabari prefers lasting, since the same root describes religion in another verse. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that this everlasting punishment is that of the Hereafter, whereas Abu Hayyan, al-Shawkani and al-Biqa'i allow that it may also take the form of repeated stonings in this world. All agree that the meteor generally burns or disables the demon without killing it. The commentators also report that demons used to listen in before the prophetic mission, and that the guarding of the sky was intensified after it. On the reading yassamma'un, al-Tabari explains that it denotes an attempt to eavesdrop rather than actual hearing.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of the description of how heaven is guarded against the devils. The exception (except one who snatches a word by stealth) refers to a devil who manages to seize a word from the angels' speech swiftly and secretly, and then a piercing meteor follows him. They broadly agree that the meteor is a bright star or fiery flame that shoots through the sky, and that the word "piercing" means shining and penetrating. Ibn 'Abbas and others say the meteor may burn the devil or disable him without killing him, while others hold that it may kill him. The verb "snatch" is explained as a quick, stealthy seizure, and the variant readings of the verb do not change the meaning much.

On what the exception attaches to, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as a substitute (badal) for the waw of the verb "they do not listen", while others treat it as a disjunctive exception. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the devils used to eavesdrop on the heavens before the prophetic mission and pass words on to soothsayers, and that the repelling became stricter after the mission. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir report that the devils climbed near the sky, listened, and then passed on what they heard, adding many lies. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the repelling was milder before the mission.

The commentators do not decide between these views; they report them as transmitted, noting that the verse does not detail how the process works. Several are content to say that this belongs to the unseen, whose reality exceeds us.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask the Meccan pagans who deny resurrection whether they are harder to create, or those whom God has created: the angels, the heavens, the earth and what lies between them. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, take the latter to mean the heavens, the earth and the mountains, with al-Razi and al-Baydawi including the angels, while Qatada understands the earlier nations. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari note that the answer is obvious: the creation of the heavens and earth is greater than that of mankind. On "clay that clings" (tin lazib), Ibn Abbas and Ikrima say it is fine, sticky clay, Qatada and Ibn Zayd say it adheres to the hand, Mujahid says it is lasting, and al-Suddi says it is pure; al-Farra' notes that the Arabs sometimes replace the letter ba with mim. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya explain that man, made of earth and water, traces back to Adam, and al-Razi concludes that the One who gave life to clay can restore it. The reading "bal 'ajibta" is debated: the majority read it with a fatha, meaning the Prophet's wonder at their denial, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and the Kufans read it with a damma, attributing the wonder to God. Shurayh rejects this reading, but al-Farra' and Ibn al-Jawzi defend it as a divine wonder meaning blame or recompense. Al-Tabari considers both readings valid.

These verses describe a challenge to those who deny the resurrection. God tells His Prophet to ask them whether they are stronger in creation, or whatever God created: the angels, the heavens and the earth. The commentators see the answer as obvious. Whoever created greater things can recreate people, who were themselves made from clay that clings, tin lazib. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree on this broad sense but differ on what "what We created" refers to. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr name the heavens, the earth and the mountains, or the angels, while others take it to mean the earlier peoples. On the meaning of lazib, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima say it means sticky or fine, Qatada and Ibn Zayd say it clings, and Mujahid says it is firm.

The phrase "bal 'ajibta wa yaskharun" is read in two ways. The majority reading with an open ta addresses the Prophet: he is astonished at their rejection, and they mock him and his astonishment. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "'ajibtu", attributing the wonder to God. Shurayh the judge rejected this reading, but al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain it as a sign of greatness or as a figure of speech, while Ibn Ashur reads it as a metaphor for strong disapproval.

Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi report that the disbelievers mocked the signs, including, according to al-Dahhak, the splitting of the moon. The phrase "a-idha mitna" expresses doubt and denial of the resurrection, to which the Prophet is to reply: "Yes, and you will be humbled."

The plain meaning of the verse is that when the idolaters are reminded of God's proofs and admonished, they do not benefit from the reminder and do not take heed; and when they see a sign confirming the Prophet's truth, they mock it. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Tabari explain that the reminder does not profit them, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to include admonition by the Quran; al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the reminder may also concern the fate of the earlier nations that were destroyed. The commentators differ on the preceding verse about wonder. Reading the verb with a damma on the taa (ʿajibtu) is attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, who take God's wonder to mean disapproval and denunciation; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe it as imagined or assumed, and Shurayh rejected this reading. Reading with a fatha on the taa (ʿajibta) addresses the Prophet, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as the Prophet's astonishment at their denial, while al-Razi reads it as wonder at their stubbornness despite clear evidence. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that the verse was revealed about Rukana and Abu al-Ashadd; al-Qurtubi distinguishes istiskhar, asking others to mock, from simple mockery. The commentators agree in portraying the idolaters' refusal and obstinacy in the face of proof.

The commentators explain that this verse describes those who turn away from proofs: when they see a sign, meaning a proof or miracle attesting to the truth of the Prophet ﷺ, they mock it. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Mujahid explain that "yastaskhirun" means to scoff and ridicule. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it to mean that they exaggerate their mockery or ask one another to scoff, a reading also given by al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi. The context concerns denial of the resurrection, and the reminders that have no effect on them.

Most cite the splitting of the moon as the sign, as Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Baghawi do, but Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and others treat this as an example rather than a limit, so the word covers any clear proof. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as a miracle showing the truth of the one who announces the resurrection. The account about Rukana is reported by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir as a possible occasion of revelation.

Readers differ over "'ajibta". The majority read it with a fatha, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: he is astonished at their denial while they mock his astonishment, a view supported by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, attributing the astonishment to God; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take this as expressing greatness or as a way of describing punishment, while Shurayh rejected it, an opinion discussed by Ibn al-Jawzi.

The disagreements therefore concern mainly the reading and its explanation, while the commentators agree on the substance: the disbelievers answer proof with mockery instead of reflection.

The commentators explain that the disbelievers called what the Prophet ﷺ brought a manifest magic, and that their denial here concerns resurrection after death, when a person becomes dust and bones. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as denial mixed with astonishment. The divine reply tells the Prophet to say: yes, you will be raised, humbled, and it will happen with a single blast, after which they will stand looking on. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'dakhirun' means humbled and abased. Al-Sa'di notes that the passage lists several astonishing attitudes of the deniers: their mockery of the signs, their refusal to take heed, and their denial framed as an emphatic question. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the second question, 'or our earlier fathers', as coordinated either with the position of 'inna' and its subject or with the pronoun in 'mab'uthun'. They note that the readings differ on the waw, some reading it with a vowel and others with silence. Concerning 'ajibta' (you wonder), the fatha reading is attributed to the Prophet and the damma reading to God. Al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari report that Shurayh rejected the damma reading, while al-Farra' and al-Bayhaqi found it preferable, understanding the wonder metaphorically. Al-Razi favours the fatha reading if the damma reading is not transmitted by mass transmission.

The commentators explain that this verse records the rejection by the idolaters of resurrection after death. They ask, in a tone of disbelief and denial, whether once they have died and become dust and bones they will be raised up again, and whether their forefathers will be too. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this as a challenge to the doctrine of resurrection, and note that these same people accepted that the first human creation came from clay. The verse then commands the Prophet to reply: yes, you will be raised, and you will be humbled. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain that 'daakhirun' means abased or humiliated, and that the 'zajra' is a single cry, the blast of the second trumpet. Their rising is then immediate, and they look on. Ibn Ashur observes that the verse follows on from the argument about God's power in the original creation. On linguistic points, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan discuss the doubled hamza and the reading of 'aw': Ibn Amir, Nafi and Abu Ja'far read it with a sukun, while the majority read it with a fatha, which strengthens the denial. The commentators agree on the main sense: the verse rejects resurrection, and the reply is the power of God.

This passage of Surat al-Saffat records the rejection of resurrection by the polytheists after death. They ask with incredulity: when we are dead and have become dust and bones, will we truly be raised, and our earliest ancestors too? The commentators read this as a rhetorical question expressing strong disbelief in the resurrection of ancestors whose bodies have long since decayed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya explain that the particle waw introduces a denying question, while the reading with a sukun on waw gives the same sense. The divine reply, delivered through the Prophet, is that they will indeed be raised, humbled, and that a single blast, the trumpet of resurrection, will suffice for them to stand up and look around. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take the blast to be the trumpet's blast. Ibn Kathir stresses that the One who created the heavens and the earth is more able to recreate mankind. Commentators also cite the verse about creation from clay: Ibn Abbas explains lazib as pure and good, Ikrima as sticky, Qatada as adhesive, and Mujahid as lasting. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that these verses were revealed concerning Abu al-Ashudd and Rukana. On the reading of the verb ʿajiba with a damma, which Hamza and al-Kisa'i followed, Shurayh rejected the idea that God is amazed, while al-Farra' defended it as an attribute of action with a meaning different from human amazement. With the fatha, the amazement is attributed to the Prophet at their disbelief and mockery.

This verse reports that the disbelievers doubted resurrection after their bodies had become dust and bones, and God tells the Prophet to answer: "Yes, you will be raised, and you will be abased." Nearly all the commentators understand "dakhirun" as humiliation and submission, with al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi noting that abasement is the greatest degree of lowliness. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi read it as a denial of resurrection, while Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as a statement that the unbelievers will be humiliated on the Day of Judgment. Regarding what follows, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the raising will happen with a single cry, the second blast of the trumpet, after which they will stand and look. Al-Hasan identifies this cry with the second blast, while al-Zamakhshari treats the pronoun "hiya" as ambiguous and clarified by the predicate that follows. Ibn 'Ashur considers the answer "yes" a response in the manner of wise discourse that redirects their rhetorical question. As for "yanzurun", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as seeing the horrors of the Last Day, al-Mawardi offers three possible meanings, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer literal seeing. Ibn Kathir adds that at the gathering the deniers will acknowledge the Day of Judgment, but that this acknowledgment will not benefit them.

This part of the verse announces that resurrection will require no delay and no repetition: it will take only one cry, the second blast of the trumpet, and people will at once be standing up alive from their graves, looking or waiting for what will be done to them. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi explain the cry as a shout or the trumpet's blast, al-Hasan specifies that it is the second blast, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that it is called a zajra because its purpose is to drive people, like a shepherd shouting at his flock.

The meaning of the verb "to look" divides the commentators. Most, such as al-Tabari, take it as seeing with the eyes: they see what they were promised, the coming of the Hour. Others, including al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy, take it to mean waiting for what will be done to them. Ibn 'Atiyya leaves both readings open, and al-Baydawi combines them. The pronoun "it" is read by al-Zamakhshari as an obscure pronoun clarified by the predicate that follows, while Abu Hayyan and others take it as referring to the resurrection.

The verse answers the mockery of the disbelievers who judged it impossible to be raised after becoming dust and bones. The commentators agree on the core point: resurrection is easy for God and happens through a single call. They differ only on the exact reference of the pronoun and the sense of the verb "to look".

This verse describes what the risen will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see what they used to deny. They call out against themselves: "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment (ad-din)." The commentators largely agree that ad-din means the day of reckoning and recompense. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada and al-Suddi, explains that God judges the servants by their deeds, and Ibn Kathir gives the same sense. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain that the word refers to repayment, as in the saying "as you do, so you will be dealt with." The exclamation "woe" (wayl) is, according to al-Zajjaj and al-Shawkani, a cry uttered at the moment of ruin; al-Farra' took it to be an older form expressing grief, which an-Nahhas rejected. On the next phrase, "This is the Day of Decision that you used to deny," the commentators differ about who speaks it. Al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani attribute it to the angels or to God addressing the disbelievers, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan allow that the disbelievers may be speaking to one another. The Day of Decision (al-fasl) is the day when God separates the people of guidance from the people of error and the good from the wicked, according to Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also note that the conjunction "and" at the start may introduce a circumstantial clause.

The verse describes the state of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection. When a single blast sounds and they rise alive, they cry out in anguish, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment." The commentators differ on who speaks the next phrase. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as addressed to the disbelievers by God, the angels, or the believers: this is the Day of Separation and judgment between creatures, the very day you used to deny. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi hold that it may be part of the disbelievers' own words to one another, or a reply from the angels; Ibn 'Atiyya notes that all agree that "This is the Day of Decision" is not spoken by the disbelievers themselves but is said to them.

There is broad agreement on the meanings of the key terms. Most commentators, such as Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, explain "al-Din" as recompense and reckoning. "Al-Fasl" is explained as the judgment and the distinction between truth and falsehood, or between the good doer and the wrongdoer, as al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur say. Al-Tabari adds that this day separates the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire.

Al-Razi notes that the disbelievers thought they were in the right, so the angels' reply shows that true recompense on that day differs from outward appearances. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur stress the reproachful tone of "that you used to deny." The overall purpose is a warning to those who denied the resurrection.

On the Day of Judgment, God commands the angels to gather those who wronged themselves through polytheism and sin, together with their counterparts. Most commentators understand the word "spouses" as their like-minded peers, so that adulterers are gathered with adulterers and drinkers with drinkers, a view attributed to Umar and Ibn Abbas. Qatada and Abu al-Aliya take it to mean their followers, al-Hasan takes it to mean their idolatrous wives, and al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it to mean their devils who were bound with them. As for what they worshipped besides God, most identify it as idols, while Muqatil says it is Iblis and his armies and al-Mawardi reports that it refers to the devils. They are then led toward the path of the Blazing Fire: Ibn Abbas explains the verb as "guide them" in the sense of pointing the way, and al-Suddi as "summon them", a form of mockery. Next they are halted for questioning. Ibn Abbas holds that they are asked about the testimony that there is no god but God, while the majority hold that they are questioned about their deeds and words. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi read the question as a rebuke: why do you not help one another, when they are now submissive and humbled. Several commentators also note the exchange in which the followers accuse their leaders of misleading them, and the leaders reply that the followers chose disbelief on their own.

This passage from Surat as-Saffat describes a scene of the Day of Judgment in which the angels are commanded to gather the wrongdoers, their like and their companions, together with what they worshipped besides God, and then to lead them to the path of the Blazing Fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take the wrongdoers to be the polytheists. Most commentators understand 'their spouses' as their counterparts in disbelief and sin: the adulterer is gathered with adulterers and the drinker of wine with drinkers, as reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Al-Hasan takes it to mean their polytheist wives, while Dahhak and Muqatil take it to mean their demon companions. As for what was worshipped, Qatada and Ikrima say idols, Muqatil says Iblis and his hosts, and others say the devils. The phrase 'guide them' is taken by most to mean point them or lead them to the way of Hell, and al-Alusi and al-Shawkani see mockery in it. Some note that al-Jahim is one of the levels of Hell. They are then halted for questioning. Opinions differ on what they will be asked about: Ibn Abbas says the testimony that there is no god but God, while the majority say their deeds and words; Ibn Abbas also mentions wronging others, and a hadith from Anas concerns one who calls others to error. On 'What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?', many see a rebuke for their helplessness, and al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi link it to Abu Jahl's boast at Badr. The verse is recited with one or two taa's. Most understand 'submitting' as yielding humbly, with no recourse left to them.

This passage of Surat as-Saffat depicts a scene from the Day of Resurrection in which God orders the angels to gather those who wronged themselves by associating partners with God, their like and companions, and what they worshipped besides God, to lead them to the path of Hell and to stop them first, because they will be questioned. The commentators differ on the subject of this questioning. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to concern their deeds and words, while al-Tabari reports that Ibn Mas'ud understood it as a mocking question about cold water, and Ibn 'Abbas in another report understood it as concerning the declaration that there is no god but God; Ad-Dahhak takes it to concern their sins. The phrase "Why do you not help one another?" is widely read as a rebuke for their inability to support each other, and it is reported that Abu Jahl said at Badr, "We are a united company who will win." The exegetes agree that the wrongdoers are the polytheists. They differ on the "spouses": 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take them to be those alike in deeds, al-Hasan and Mujahid take them to be idolatrous women, and Ad-Dahhak and Muqatil take them to be devils who accompanied them. Several cite the hadith of Anas that whoever calls to something will be held with it on the Day of Resurrection. Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the "submitting" are those humbled and unable to defend themselves, and that the followers and the leaders blame each other for the misguidance.

This passage from Surat as-Saffat describes the scene of the Day of Judgment: the angels are commanded to gather the wrongdoers, their likes, and what they worshipped besides God, then to halt them for questioning. The words "What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?" are a rebuke and mockery: why do they not support each other as they claimed in the world? The commentators see in this a recall of Abu Jahl's boast at Badr: "We are a victorious host." The implied answer is powerlessness: they are "submitting", humbled and without recourse, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada explain. Opinions differ on the subject of the questioning: Ibn Abbas, Yahya ibn Salam and Muqatil take it to concern the testimony "There is no god but God", al-Dahhak takes it to concern their sins, and the majority hold it concerns their deeds and words, while some regard the rebuke itself as the question. The meaning of "spouses" is also debated: Umar, Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as their peers, such as usurers with usurers; al-Hasan takes it as idolatrous wives; Muqatil and al-Dahhak as their demon companions. As for "the right hand", Qatada and Ibn Abbas read it as the side of good counsel, Ibn al-Jawzi as oaths, and others as strength. The following verses, in which followers and leaders shift the blame onto one another, carry this meaning forward.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Judgment in which the disbelievers are halted and questioned in reproach: why do they not help one another as they did in the world? The answer is that today they are submitting, meaning humbled and unable to defend themselves. The commentators agree on the core sense of humiliation and helplessness. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada explain that they are abased or submissive under God's punishment, al-Akhfash says they throw down their hands, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the submission as obedience to God's decree. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that some abandoned others out of helplessness, so all are submissive and none can prevail. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the question as mockery and rebuke, answering Abu Jahl's boast at Badr that they were a united, victorious company. The passage continues with followers and leaders blaming one another. The followers say the leaders came to them from the right, which the scholars explain as by oath, by promises of good, or by force, while the leaders reply that they were not believers to begin with and had no authority over them. On the meaning of the spouses, Ibn Abbas, Umar and al-Nu'man ibn Bashir take them as their like and kind in sin, al-Hasan and Mujahid as the idolatrous wives, and al-Dahhak and Muqatil as the devils who accompanied them. Regarding those worshipped besides God, some name the idols and others the devils or Iblis. The verse shows that polytheism and sin gather their people together in the hereafter, and that worshippers and their objects of worship cannot help one another.

This verse depicts a scene on the Day of Resurrection: after the disbelievers are halted, questioned, and left unable to help one another, they turn to one another and exchange accusations. The commentators agree that this questioning is one of rebuke and blame rather than an innocent inquiry. Opinions differ on who the speakers are: Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take them to be humans and jinn, or disbelievers and their devils, while Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take them to be the followers and their leaders. Ibn 'Abbas explains the verb as mutual blame; others read it as seeking comfort, a view al-Mawardi rejects, since the people of the Fire receive no rest. The followers tell their leaders, "You used to come at us from the right." Its meaning is debated: for Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others it is force and compulsion; for Mujahid and al-Hasan it is truth and religion; for some it is the oaths by which they were deceived; for 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd it is the direction of safety and blessing. The leaders reply that they never made the followers disbelieve, that they had no power over them, and that the followers were rebellious by their own choice. By their own admission, all of them deserve the punishment, and they share it just as they shared the misguidance.

This verse depicts a scene on the Day of Judgment in which the followers and their leaders blame one another for their misguidance. The followers tell their leaders that they used to come to them "from the right", which most commentators understand to mean that they turned them away from the truth and made falsehood appealing. The commentators offer several readings of "the right" (al-yamin). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Farra', al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean force and compulsion, citing the line of al-Shammakh about 'Arabah al-Awsi. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd understand it as the good and the truth, while al-Kalbi and Ibn Khusayf read it as the right direction or the favourable side. Others take it to refer to the oaths that the leaders swore to their followers, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention worldly pleasures and wealth. The leaders reply that the followers were never believers to begin with, that they exercised no coercion or proof over them, and that the followers themselves were the transgressors. The commentators agree that both sides acknowledge deserving the punishment and share it just as they shared the error. Ibn Kathir and al-Biqa'i link the scene to the mutual accusations in the place of gathering, while Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi stress the note of reproach. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that the interpreters differ considerably on the meaning of "from the right", which accounts for the range of views, though all of them converge on the idea of deception and seduction.

This passage describes a dialogue that takes place at the gathering on the Day of Resurrection between the followers and their leaders, among both jinn and humans. The followers reproach their leaders, saying that they used to come to them "from the right", meaning from the side of religion and truth, to turn them away from it and make falsehood look attractive. Commentators differ on what "the right" means. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Farra', al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as force and compulsion, citing a line of al-Shammakh; Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd understand it as goodness and truth; Mujahid takes it as the truth that the leaders claimed to be on; al-Kalbi, al-Zajjaj and al-Dahhak take it as religion or as deception and seduction; others take it as the oaths the leaders swore to their followers, as al-Mawardi and al-Nisaburi report. Ibn 'Atiyya considers these meanings close and possible together without choosing between them. The leaders reply that the followers were never believers to begin with, that they were not forced, and that the leaders had no authority over them, but that they were rebellious people who chose disbelief, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud explain. Most commentators read the phrase "the word of our Lord has come true against us, and we shall taste the punishment" as a statement that all of them will suffer it, and read the leading astray as an invitation rather than compulsion. Ibn 'Atiyya also notes that the speakers may be jinn and humans, or simply disbelievers, and that several interpretations may coexist.

This passage recounts a dialogue on the Day of Resurrection between the followers and their leaders, among humans and jinn, as they blame one another for their misguidance. The followers say that the leaders used to come to them from the right, that is, from the side of truth and good, and turned them away from it, or overpowered them by their strength. The leaders reply that they had never been believers, and that they had no authority, proof, or compulsion over them: it was the followers themselves who were transgressors, by their own choice. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'the right'. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatada take it to mean force or the side of goodness; al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read it as a metaphor for strength, goodness, oaths or pleasures; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list other senses, such as seduction and deception. The word 'authority' (sultan) is also explained in different ways: al-Suddi takes it as proof, while others take it as force or coercion. All agree that disbelief came from the free choice of its people and not from compulsion, and that all will share the punishment, though to different degrees according to their deeds. Ibn Kathir reports that this confrontation recurs in Hell. The passage then turns to the arrogance of those who refused the declaration of faith and called the Prophet a poet or a madman; God answers that he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers before him.

This passage of Surat as-Saffat recounts the dispute among the people of the Fire on the Day of Judgment, when followers and leaders blame one another. The followers tell their leaders that they used to come to them "from the right". Ibn Abbas explains this as coercion and force, while Qatada, Ibn Zayd and others take it to mean the path of good from which they were turned away, Mujahid as the truth, al-Hasan as the lure of desires, wealth and deception, and some as oaths and pledges. The leaders reply that the followers were never believers to begin with and that they had no authority to compel them; the rebellion was the followers' own, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi. Both sides then acknowledge that their Lord's word has come true and that all of them will taste the punishment, and the leaders admit they misled others because they themselves were misguided. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that their shared punishment reflects their shared error, and that God deals with each criminal according to his deeds. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others report that the arrogant refused to say "there is no god but God" and called the Prophet ﷺ a mad poet; God answers that he brought the truth and confirmed the earlier messengers. The passage closes with the painful punishment awaiting the guilty and the known provision promised to the sincere servants of God. The commentators agree on divine justice and on punishment matching deeds, while differing on the precise meaning of several terms.

The commentators explain that these verses recount the exchange between followers and leaders, jinn and humans, on the Day of Resurrection. The leaders admit that the punishment is due to them and that they led their followers astray because they themselves were astray. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree on the apparent meaning of inciting others to error, and that all share the punishment in proportion to their share in the error, which is the lot of every criminal. The meaning of "from the right" has several explanations: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' take it as force and compulsion, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd as the good or its path, Mujahid as the truth, al-Hasan as worldly wealth, and Ibn 'Atiyya suggests it may refer to the oaths they swore. As for the phrase "you were not believers," Qatada attributes it to the devils, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin attribute it to the leaders, who tell the followers that they chose disbelief themselves. Al-Baghawi notes that "sharers in the punishment" refers to leaders and followers together. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report that the disbelievers turned away from the declaration "There is no god but God" and called the Prophet a possessed poet; the divine reply affirms that he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers before him. Commentators show no major disagreement on this point.

This verse states that the misguided and those who misguided them, followers and leaders alike, will share the same punishment on the Day of Resurrection, just as they shared in error and disobedience in this world. It belongs to a dialogue among the disbelievers: the leaders admit that they led their followers astray, and the followers blame them for having turned them away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand this exchange as taking place between jinn and humans, Qatada restricts it to humans and jinn, while Ibn Zayd and Mujahid see it as between humans and their devils.

The commentators agree that sharing the punishment does not mean equality. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that each receives according to his deeds, and Ibn 'Ashur suggests that those who led others astray may suffer more. The phrase "you used to come to us from the right" divides opinion: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read it as force and compulsion, al-Hasan and al-Suddi as the path of good or truth, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi as religion or deceptive oaths, and Ibn Jarir as the deceptive route by which people were turned away.

The leaders reply that they had no power to compel their followers and that these were already inclined to disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin draw from this that people act by their own choice. The passage continues with the disbelievers' refusal of the declaration "There is no god but God," and their charge that the Prophet is a poet or a madman, which the Qur'an rejects.

This verse states that God deals with the wrongdoers in the same way as the scene just described: followers and leaders, who blame one another on the Day of Resurrection, share the same punishment. Most commentators understand the wrongdoers (mujrimun) as polytheists, and their crime as associating others with God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the speakers are jinn and humans, or weak followers and powerful leaders, and that the phrase "you used to come to us from the right" may mean force and compulsion, good that was turned away, religion, oaths, or desires; al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari develop several of these senses, while Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that sharing the punishment does not mean equal degrees of suffering. The commentators agree that the sentence is just and matches the deed. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani report that these unbelievers were arrogant when told "there is no god but God", and called the Prophet a poet or a madman; God answers that he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers before him. Al-Jaza'iri and the King Fahd text summarise the verse as a punishment for those who chose disobedience. Other passages in the same scene describe the reward of the sincere servants of God: a known provision of fruits, honour in gardens of bliss, and drink that does not intoxicate.

This verse describes the Meccan polytheists who became arrogant whenever they were told to say, "There is no god but God." They dismissed the Prophet ﷺ as a mad poet, and God replies that he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers before him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur agree that the phrase is the declaration of Divine unity, which the disbelievers refused out of pride. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that the formula is recommended to be taught to the dying.

The meaning of "yamin" (right hand) is explained in several ways. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Zamakhshari take it as force and compulsion, Mujahid as the truth, al-Hasan as wealth and desires, and others as oaths and pledges. The commentators also differ over who speaks: Mujahid says the disbelievers address the devils, Qatada says humans address jinn, and others say the followers address their leaders.

The leaders reply that they had no power over their followers and that the followers chose misguidance themselves. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Uthaymin note that this shared blame explains why all share the punishment, though each according to his deeds.

The passage then describes the reward of the sincere servants: a known provision, fruits, a pure drink without intoxication or harm, and modest-gazing spouses. Ibn Abbas and al-Tabari give varying readings of the word "ghawl" (harm), some taking it as headache or stomach pain and others as any harm or sin.

This verse reports the words of the Meccan disbelievers about the Prophet ﷺ when the call to monotheism was presented to them: shall we abandon our gods for a mad poet? The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, agree that the subject of «they say» is the idolaters of Mecca, and that «a mad poet» refers to the Prophet ﷺ. God's reply, «Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers», is understood as a rejection of this charge: he brought the truth, the Qur'an and monotheism, and what he brings agrees with what the earlier messengers brought. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that his confirmation of the messengers means he brought what they had announced, while Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes two aspects: the fulfilment of their prophecies about his coming, and the agreement of his message with theirs.

Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di, connect the passage to the formula «There is no god but God», which the proud disbelievers refused to utter. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said he was commanded to fight people until they say it. Regarding the word «yamin» in the following verse, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note several meanings: power and compulsion, the direction of good, or oaths; al-Mawardi lists eight. The readings also differ on «al-mukhlasin»: the readers of Medina and Kufa read it with a fatha, meaning those whom God has purified, while the others read it with a kasra, meaning those who made their worship sincerely for God.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the Quraysh who called the Prophet ﷺ a mad poet and refused to abandon their gods for his sake. The reply is that he was neither a poet nor insane, but came with the truth, namely the message of monotheism and the Quran. Al-Tabari and Qatada take this as a divine statement refuting the idolaters, with the truth identified as the Quran revealed to him. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud understand his confirming the messengers to mean that his message agrees with what the earlier messengers brought, above all the call to monotheism. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Attiya offer a different reading in which the confirmation lies in the earlier prophets having announced his coming, and in the match between his message and theirs. Al-Razi notes that the truth is the upright religion established by reason and proof. The commentators agree on the general sense that the charges of poetry and madness are baseless, and differ only on how the confirmation should be understood and what it includes. Al-Qurtubi also records the readings of the phrase about those who taste the painful punishment with nasb or khafd.

This verse tells the polytheists who denied the message that they will taste the painful punishment, and that they will be repaid only for what they used to do. The commentators note that the emphasis with inna and the lam confirms the certainty of the warning, and that the shift from the third person to the second is meant to show God's anger and to rebuke the guilty directly. They agree that the recompense matches the deed. The verse follows the scene where the followers and their leaders blame one another. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the exception, "except the sincere servants of God", refers to the monotheist believers who will not taste this punishment; Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi treat it as a disjunctive exception. On the reading, the majority read "dha'iqu" with the nun dropped and "al-adhab" in the genitive, while Abu al-Sammal read the accusative, and Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi mention that this is a recognized construction in Arabic. Ibn Kathir stresses that the verb "taste" means the punishment is real and certain. The scholars do not differ on the general meaning, only on the detail of the exception and the reading. The verse introduces the description of the bliss promised to the sincere, set in contrast with the fate of the guilty, in the Quranic manner of joining hope and fear.

God declares that the disbelievers who associated partners with Him and denied His messengers will taste the painful punishment, and that they will be repaid only for what they used to do, with no injustice. The commentators agree that this address is directed at the polytheists, and that the exception that follows concerns the sincere monotheist believers. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tabari stress that divine justice requires recompense proportionate to the deed. Al-Alusi and al-Biqa'i observe that the use of the word "deeds" for the recompense implies that it is of the same nature as the act. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the exception as disjunctive, meaning that the believers do not undergo this punishment, while others take it as continuous when the address is generalized. Scholars differ on the scope of the repayment: some limit it to evil deeds, while Ibn 'Ashur extends it to all blameworthy words and conduct. As for the description that follows of the blessings reserved for the sincere, including the known provision, the fruits, and the white cup that causes no intoxication, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri explain it as a reward far exceeding the deeds performed. The shared conclusion is the affirmation of divine justice and a warning against polytheism.

In this verse God makes an exception to the painful punishment suffered by the disbelievers and the misguided: His sincere servants, those who devoted their faith and worship purely to Him and whom He chose for His mercy. These do not taste the punishment and are repaid with a favour that exceeds their deeds. The commentators agree that this exception is disjunctive, meaning 'but', so that God's sincere servants are not like the others. They explain that these will have a known provision in Paradise, fruits they enjoy for pleasure rather than sustenance, and that they will be honoured in gardens of bliss, reclining face to face on couches, while attendants serve them a flowing cup of pure, white wine, delicious to drinkers, which brings neither harm nor intoxication. The scholars differ on the meaning of ghawl: Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as headache, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd as stomach ache, as-Suddi as the seizing of reason, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as any harm at all; al-Tabari holds that the negation encompasses all these afflictions. The word yunzafun is read in two ways: with a fatha it means their minds will not be taken away by drink; with a kasra, that their drink will not run out. Al-Tabari considers both readings valid and close in meaning. The houris with restrained gaze and wide eyes are likened to a well-guarded ostrich egg; some take this to be a pearl in its shell, al-Hasan an ostrich egg hidden under its feathers, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Tabari the inner part of the egg before it is touched.

This passage from Surat as-Saffat describes what awaits the sincere servants of God in Paradise, in contrast with the painful punishment reserved for those who associate partners with God. The commentators agree that the 'known provision' is the sustenance of Paradise, given to them morning and evening, as another verse states. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the fruits are whatever is eaten for pleasure rather than for sustenance, since the bodies of the people of Paradise are made to last forever. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tabari report that 'honour' means being served and cared for. The cup is the vessel holding the drink, and several scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash, held that every 'cup' in the Quran means wine. All agree that the wine of Paradise is free from the harms of worldly wine, such as headache and loss of reason. The scholars differ on the meaning of 'ghawl': Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it as headache, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd as stomach pain, as-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayda as the drink seizing the mind, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as any harm at all. At-Tabari considers that all these meanings fall under the negation. On the reading of 'yunzafun', some read it with a fatha and understand that their minds are not carried away, while others read it with a kasra and understand that the drink does not run out or that they do not become drunk. The 'women of restrained glance' are the wives who look only upon their husbands. For the 'guarded eggs', al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd compare them to ostrich eggs, as-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr to the white inside of an egg before its shell is removed, and Ibn 'Abbas to the protected pearl. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir adopt as-Suddi's view.

The plain meaning of the verse is that the sincere servants of God will have a known provision of fruits, and that they will be honoured in the Gardens of Delight. The commentators explain that the provision described as fruits refers to what is eaten for pleasure rather than to sustain the body, since the bodies of the people of Paradise are firm and everlasting. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that fruits means all kinds of fruit, fresh and dried, and that the honour is what God bestows on them. They differ on the meaning of known provision: Qatada took it to be Paradise itself, others the provision within it, others a fixed time such as morning and evening, and others a fixed measure. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the honour means the provision reaches them without toil or request, unlike the provision of this world. The commentaries then address the cup of wine that carries no ghawl and does not intoxicate. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya record several meanings of ghawl, namely a headache, a stomach ache, the bewilderment of the mind, or sin. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say these meanings are close and that the general principle is to deny any harm. The commentators also note differing readings of the word yunzafun among the reciters. These differences are reported without any scholar being preferred over another.

أما القاصرات الطرف فقد فسرها أكثر المفسرين بأنهن نساء قصرن أبصارهن على أزواجهن، وفسرها بعضهم بأنهن محبوسات على أزواجهن، والحور العين شبهت ببيض النعام المكنون، وذهب الحسن وابن زيد إلى أن المراد بيض النعام، وذهب سعيد بن جبير والسدي إلى أنه بطن البيضة أو القشرة الداخلية، ومع ذلك فالمفسرون متفقون على أن نعيم الجنة مستور عن الإدراك الدنيوي، وأن لذة الشراب والمجالسة والتكريم داخلة كلها في النعيم الموصوف.

This verse describes how the sincere believers, chosen by God, sit in Paradise: on raised couches, facing one another. Most commentators understand the 'facing one another' to mean that no one sees the back of his companion, which, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, makes their joy and intimacy more complete. Al-Qurtubi reports another view, that the couches turn with their occupants so that no one sees another's back. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur see in it chiefly a sign of affection and fellowship, with each group gathered according to its rank. Ibn Juzayy adds that this facing may be for conversation, while at other times each person withdraws to his own palace. Abu Hayyan notes that the word 'surur' is read with either a fatha or a damma, both being accepted. Al-Alusi recalls a hadith that the veils are sometimes lifted so that each one looks at his companion. On the meaning of the verse itself the commentators do not really disagree: they all agree that it describes serene intimacy, complete courtesy and perfect happiness.

This verse describes the drink of the people of Paradise. A cup is passed around them in their gatherings, filled with wine that flows like visible springs. Most commentators, beginning with Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash, take the word kas to mean the wine itself or the vessel holding it, and it is reported that every mention of a cup in the Quran refers to wine. Al-Hasan al-Basri says this wine is whiter than milk, while Ibn Mas'ud's reading has yellow. The commentators agree that this drink is free of the harms of worldly wine: there is no ghawl in it, meaning it causes no harm, no sickness and no intoxication. On the meaning of ghawl the views differ. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as headache, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd as stomach ache, al-Sha'bi and Abu 'Ubayda as the seizing of the mind, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as any harm or discomfort. al-Tabari prefers a general negation covering all these senses. As for the verb yunzafun, read with an open or a kasra zay, the readings differ without real contradiction: the first means they are not left without their minds by drink, the second that their drink does not run out, and al-Tabari holds both readings to be equally sound.

This verse describes the drink passed round to the people of Paradise: it is white in colour and a delight to those who drink it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the word kas to mean the drink itself, citing al-Dahhak that every kas in the Qur'an means wine, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that it refers to the vessel holding the drink. On the colour, al-Hasan al-Basri says the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk, and a reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud has "yellow". Al-Tabari explains that the feminine adjective agrees with the feminine noun kas.

The commentators agree that this wine is free of the harms of worldly wine. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take ghawl to mean headache or stomach ache; al-Hasan says headache, al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi say it means that the drink does not seize their minds, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it means any harm or hurt. For yunzafun, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra, and Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand it as their minds not being taken away. Al-Fara' and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it may also mean the drink will never run out. Al-Tabari judges both readings correct and close in meaning: they will not be drunk.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan add that God has cleansed this wine of headache, pains, vomiting and intoxication, while its delight remains complete and free of any aftertaste.

This verse states that the wine of Paradise has no ghawl, a hidden harm that corrupts body or mind as wine does in this world, and that its drinkers are not yunzafun, meaning deprived of their reason by intoxication. Most commentators understand ghawl as an insidious, destructive harm, so the verse negates all the ills of wine. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take these to be headache or stomach pain, while al-Sudi and Abu Ubayda take it to mean that the wine does not steal the mind. Al-Kalbi says it means sin, and al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi offer other closely related readings. As for the verb yunzafun, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the zay, the others with a fatha. With the fatha, the meaning is that they are not intoxicated and do not lose their reason; with the kasra, the meaning is that their drink does not run out. Al-Tabari judges both readings correct and compatible, while al-Nahhas and Ibn Kathir find the fatha reading clearer. Al-Farra' notes that the kasra reading may also mean that the drink never ends. The commentators thus agree that the wine of Paradise is free of the harms of worldly wine, but they differ on what exactly those harms are.

This verse describes the women of Paradise as "restrainers of the glance", that is, they fix their eyes only on their husbands and look at no one else, and as having large, beautiful eyes. The commentators agree on the general sense: al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd that they look only at their spouses, and Ibn Zayd adds that a woman there tells her husband she sees nothing finer than him. On the word 'in, al-Samani, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean beautiful eyes, while al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd understand large eyes, and al-Hasan a marked whiteness of the eye with deep blackness of the pupil. On the simile of the "hidden eggs" the views differ: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatada and al-Tabari take it to be the inner membrane of the shell, which al-Tabari prefers for its fineness; al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to be an ostrich egg protected by its feathers, tinged with yellow; Ibn 'Abbas takes it to be the pearl within its shell; 'Ata' names the thin layer between the outer shell and the white. Several lexicographers note that the Arabs compare a beautiful woman to an ostrich egg, a complexion they regard as the finest among women.

This verse describes the women of Paradise as chaste, their gaze restricted to their husbands, with large and beautiful eyes, and with a veiled, pure complexion likened to eggs kept hidden. The commentators agree that "restricting the gaze" means that these women look only at their husbands, and that "'in" is the plural of "'ayna", a woman with wide, beautiful eyes, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi are reported to have said and as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi record. On the comparison with eggs, opinions differ. Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and most exegetes take it to mean ostrich eggs, shielded by their feathers from dust and wind, whose whiteness tends toward a pale yellow, which the Arabs considered the finest complexion in women, and they cite the verses of Imru' al-Qays. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi and al-Tabari understand the inner part of the shell, or its whiteness beneath the membrane before it is touched by hands, and al-Tabari prefers this view because the outer layer is touched by birds and hands. Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, and al-Akhfash understand pearls within their shell. Most commentators note that the Arabs called women "eggs of the curtained tents". No one decisively settles the matter, and some combine these interpretations.

This verse describes the people of Paradise once they are seated on couches facing one another, turning to ask each other about their lives in the world. The commentators link the phrase to the serving of drinks: they drink and converse as companions do at a feast, yet the meaning is a conversation of ease and delight. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that it is the people of Paradise who question one another about their past circumstances. Within this exchange one of them mentions a companion in the world who denied the Resurrection. The commentators differ on who this companion was: Mujahid says he was a devil, Ibn 'Abbas a disbelieving partner, Muqatil a brother, and others the two men mentioned in the chapter of the Cave. Ibn Kathir holds that a devil and a human are not contradictory here. The reading 'al-musaddiqin' with a shadda is noted by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan as a reading of charity, but an-Nahhas and Ibn al-Jawzi reject it as not fitting the meaning. According to Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar, there are openings in Paradise through which one may look down at Hell; the believer sees his companion in the middle of the blaze, rebukes him for having nearly ruined him, and thanks God for his guidance. Opinions differ on the phrase 'Are we not to die, except our first death?': some take it as joy at everlasting life, others as a rebuke addressed to the companion. Ibn Jarir takes the closing words 'for the like of this let the workers work' as God's speech, while others attribute them to the people of Paradise.

This passage describes the conversation of the people of Paradise, reclining and enjoying their drink, as they recall their past lives on earth. One of them says he once had a companion who denied the resurrection and mocked him for believing it, asking how people could be raised after becoming dust and bones to face reckoning and reward. He then invites his companions to look down into the Fire to see that companion. He sees him in the midst of the Blaze, rebukes him for nearly destroying him, and thanks God for His blessing, saying that without it he would have been among those brought to punishment. He returns to his companions to affirm that they will not die again after their first death and will not be punished, calling it the supreme triumph and urging others to work for the like of it. The commentators largely agree on the core meaning. Mujahid identifies the companion as a devil, Ibn 'Abbas as an associate or companion, either a believer or disbeliever, Muqatil says they were two brothers, and al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi note that some hold they are the two men of the Cave chapter. Ibn Kathir and most others understand the resurrection as reckoning and recompense. The word 'madinun' is glossed as 'judged' or 'recompensed', with Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b explaining it as repayment for deeds. The majority reading 'al-musaddiqin' is contrasted with a reading 'al-mutasaddiqin' meaning those who give charity; al-Tabari says the account of the second partner supports that reading, though he prefers the lighter form. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi relate the story of the man who gave away his wealth and then refused to help a brother in need. Ibn Kathir and Qatada report that Paradise has openings through which its people look down on the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the speaker might be God or an angel, but most commentators take it to be the believer himself.

This verse records the words of one of the people of Paradise recalling a companion he had in the world, who mocked him and denied the Resurrection: "Are you indeed among those who affirm it? When we are dead and become dust and bones, shall we really be requited?" The commentators agree that this is a question of reproach and disbelief, set within the pleasure the people of Paradise take in conversing over their drinks. On the identity of the companion, opinions differ: Mujahid says it was Satan, Ibn 'Abbas and al-'Awfi say it was a polytheist who had a believing friend, Muqatil says they were two brothers, and others say they were two business partners, the pair whose story is told in the chapter of the Cave. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relay a long account attributed to Furat ibn Tha'laba about these partners, which Ibn Kathir notes belongs to Israelite narratives. On the reading of "al-musaddiqin", al-Tabari upholds the common reading meaning belief in the Resurrection, while some read it as those who give charity and argue the story of the partners supports this; al-Nahhas and al-Zajjaj reject that reading. Most explain "madinun" as "recompensed" or "called to account", and some as "governed". As for "hal antum mutta'iluna", some take it as the speaker's question to his companions, others as the words of the angels or of God, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b report that Paradise has openings through which its people can look at Hell. The believer then sees his companion in the midst of the blaze, accuses him of nearly ruining him, and thanks God for having guided him.

The verse recounts what the people of Paradise say to one another as they recline in comfort, recalling their past lives. One of them says that in the world he had a companion who denied the Resurrection and mocked him for believing it. That companion had asked in disbelief: when we die and become dust and bones, will we really be recompensed and called to account? The commentators explain that "madinun" means judged or repaid, and that the question is one of denial. The commentators differ on who this companion was. Mujahid says it was Satan, Ibn Abbas says it was a disbelieving partner, Muqatil says they were two brothers, and several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, identify them as the two partners mentioned in the chapter of the Cave. Al-Tabari notes that this account supports the reading with a shadda on the sad, while the widely accepted reading without it remains the standard one. The speaker then asks his companions whether they wish to look down into the Fire.
