He sees his former companion in the middle of the blaze and tells him that he nearly destroyed him, and that only his Lord's grace kept him from being among those brought there. The people of Paradise then say there is no death for them, that this is the great triumph, and that those who strive should work for the like of it. Some commentators take the last sentence as God's words, others as the words of the people of Paradise.

This passage recounts what the people of Paradise say to one another once they are settled on their couches, recalling their lives in this world. One of them says that he had a companion in the world who denied the resurrection and mocked the idea of being recompensed. He then asks his companions whether they would like to look down into the Fire with him to see that companion. He looks and sees him in the midst of the Blazing Fire. He addresses him with a rebuke: he nearly destroyed him through his misguidance, and it was only God's favour that kept him from being among those brought forth for punishment. Turning back to his companions, he states that they will not die again and will not be tormented, and he regards this as the great triumph, calling on people to work for the like of it. The commentators agree on the core meaning, namely the looking down upon the people of the Fire, and note that some hold that Paradise has openings through which its inhabitants can look. They differ on who is speaking: some say it is the believer addressing his companions, others that it is God or an angel offering the people of Paradise this view. They also differ on the identity of the companion. Mujahid says he was a devil, Ibn 'Abbas and others say he was a human associate who disbelieved, Muqatil says they were brothers, and many link the story to the parable of the two men in the Surah of the Cave. Ibn Kathir and others cite narratives of Israelite origin on this point. Variant readings do not change the main sense, and most explain that the word radā means ruin or perdition.

This passage of Surat al-Saffat describes a conversation among the people of Paradise. One of them recalls a companion from worldly life who denied the Resurrection and mocked his belief; he then asks his companions whether they would like to look down at the Fire with him to see that man's fate. He looks and sees the companion in the midst of the Blazing Fire, and tells him that he almost destroyed him by leading him astray, were it not for his Lord's blessing. The commentators agree that "sawa' al-jahim" means the middle of Hell, a term applied to the midst because the distance from it to the sides is equal, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Tabari and others. They differ on who the companion was: Mujahid says a devil, Ibn Abbas a disbelieving partner, Muqatil two brothers, and many link the two men to the people of the Cave in the sura of al-Kahf. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others note a reading attributed to some reciters, "muṭli'ūnī" with a kasra, which al-Tabari considers irregular because Arabs do not attach a pronoun to this form in that way, while Ibn Jinni defends it by treating the active participle as an imperfect. As for the words "Are we not dying, except our first death?", some take them as the words of the people of Paradise when death is slaughtered, others as thankfulness for eternal life, and others as a rebuke to the companion. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'labi relate lengthy accounts of two Israelite partners concerning the spending of wealth, which Ibn Kathir notes come from Israelite narratives. Finally, "For the like of this, let the workers work" is attributed by Qatada to the people of Paradise, and by Ibn Jarir to God Himself, the sense being that such bliss deserves that people labour for it.

This verse records the words of the believer in Paradise to his former companion who, in the world, denied the resurrection. After looking down and seeing him in the midst of Hellfire, he says: by God, you almost ruined me, and had it not been for my Lord's favour, I would have been among those brought forth to punishment. The commentators agree that 'radd' means destruction, and that the companion almost led the believer to ruin. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take this companion to be either a devil or an unbelieving man; others say he was a partner, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate the story of the two partners mentioned in Surat al-Kahf, while Ibn Kathir also transmits narrations from the Israelite traditions. Ibn Mas'ud read 'to lead you astray'. al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad explain the sense as perishing or being cast into the fire. al-Farra' and al-Mawardi note that 'muhdarin' is used only for evil, meaning those dragged to punishment. As for 'are we not dead except for our first death?', most take it as the words of the people of Paradise rejoicing in their eternal life, while some take it as a rebuke to the companion. The great success mentioned next is the reward that calls the doers to act. The readings differ on the verb 'muttali'un' and on the interrogative hamzas, and the commentators do not decide between them.

This passage from Surat As-Saffat describes the people of Paradise, reclining on couches and talking about their earthly lives. One of them recalls that he had a companion in the world who denied the resurrection and doubted that people would be repaid once they had become dust and bones. He then invites his companions to look down into the Fire with him, and he sees that companion in the middle of the blaze. He tells him that he nearly destroyed him by leading him astray, and that only the grace of his Lord, through guidance and protection, kept him from being brought to punishment alongside him. The commentators explain that a person is saved only through God's grace and success, and that the grace here means faith and steadfastness in it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that tardin means that you would ruin me, and that those brought forth are those led to punishment, while al-Mawardi notes that the verb ahdara is used only for evil. They differ on the identity of the companion: Mujahid takes him to be a devil, Ibn Abbas a disbelieving partner, others a brother or a human, and several link the story to the account of the two men in Surat al-Kahf. Readers also differ on how the word for those who confirm is pronounced, and on how one looks into the Fire, some reporting that Paradise has openings through which the fire can be seen. As for the words 'Shall we not die, except our first death?', some attribute them to the people of Paradise when death is slaughtered, others read them as an expression of joy at the lasting of their bliss, and others as a rebuke addressed to the companion.

This verse reports the words of the people of Paradise, who rejoice and marvel at their everlasting state: "Are we not to die, save our first death, and will we not be punished?" The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, read it as an expression of joy and gratitude from a believer who is certain he will neither die again nor be tormented. Al-Tabari cites Qatada as saying these are the words of the people of Paradise.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain the initial fa as linked to an implied sentence, roughly: "Are we then blessed and everlasting, so that we will neither die nor be punished?" They add that the believers' lot is to taste only the first death, unlike the disbelievers who wish for death every hour. Al-Razi notes that these words may have been spoken before the death is slaughtered in Paradise, or that they may come from the amazement of someone who fears his happiness will not last.

The scholars disagree about the speaker. Many hold that it is the believer addressing his companions in Paradise; al-Nasafi holds it may be addressed to his former companion in the Fire, as a rebuke. Ibn 'Atiyya accepts both readings. Ibn Kathir relates a narration about death being slaughtered as a ram, which he presents with some caution. On the next verse, "For the like of this, let the workers work", Qatada takes it as the words of the people of Paradise, al-Tabari as God's words to humans, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers that it may be an exhortation to work, though the hereafter is not a place of work. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi also mention a rare reading, "bi-ma'itin".

This verse records the words of the people of Paradise, rejoicing in their immortality. One of them asks, in delight, whether they will not die again beyond their first death, and whether they will not be punished. Most commentators read this as a rhetorical question expressing gratitude rather than seeking an answer. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present it as the speech of the people of Paradise celebrating eternal dwelling. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the fa' is linked to an omitted clause, meaning: are we then immortal and blessed, so that we will not die nor be punished? Al-Razi reports that it may have been said before the people of Paradise knew they would never die, and then again once Death is slaughtered in the form of a ram. Others, such as al-Alusi, note that the speaker may be addressing his companions, while al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya suggest he may be rebuking his former companion in the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir also note that the phrase "for the like of this let the workers work" has been attributed to the believer, to the angels, or to God addressing the faithful. Commentators agree that escape from punishment together with lasting bliss is a great triumph, and that the verse urges good works. They differ on who is addressed, with some taking it as the believer's fellows in Paradise and others as the former companion in the Fire.

This verse expresses the joy of the people of Paradise at an eternal bliss: they are free from death and punishment, and this, they say, is the great triumph. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these words are spoken by the people of Paradise among themselves, rejoicing in God's favours. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi add that the believer may say them to his unbelieving companion, who denied the resurrection, as a rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that they may also be God's own words confirming what they said. Ibn Juzayy considers it more likely that these are God's words, since they connect with what follows. Ibn 'Ashur sees the question as a confirmation meant to recall the grace of immortality. As for the next phrase, 'For the like of this let the workers work', Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir attribute it either to the people of Paradise or to God, urging good deeds in this life. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that the Hereafter is not a place of work, so the phrase must be understood figuratively. Ibn Kathir also reports a long narration, drawn from Israelite traditions, about two partners, one generous and one stingy, which illustrates the verse. The commentators do not decide between these readings.

This part of the verse describes the people of Paradise, who, seated on couches facing one another, recall their lives in this world and the success they have attained. The plain meaning that the commentators share is that such an enduring bliss and great triumph should move people to act in order to attain it. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, hold that the phrase "For the like of this let the workers work" is God's own word, exhorting people to seek His reward through obedience. Qatada, however, attributes it to the people of Paradise, and others take it as the words of the believer himself. Al-Tabari explains the "great triumph" as deliverance from the punishment of God that they had feared in the world, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi stress the lasting nature of this bliss. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that "the like of this" may refer to the honour and comfort described just before. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur understand the command to act as an incitement to righteous deeds in this life, while the verse as a whole calls for obedience and sincerity, in contrast with the fate of the disbelievers mentioned in the context.

In this verse God poses a rhetorical question of reproach: is this bliss described for the people of Paradise, their hospitality (nuzul), better, or the tree of zaqqum, the food of the people of the Fire? Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi explain nuzul as abundance and the produce of food, while al-Zamakhshari and others hold that what comes from the promised provision is joy and delight, whereas what comes from the zaqqum is pain and grief; the comparison serves to rebuke the disbelievers for their poor choice, since the zaqqum has no good in it at all. The scholars differ over the nature of the zaqqum: Qutrub and others describe a bitter, harmful tree growing in Tihama, while others say it is unknown among the trees of this world and grows at the bottom of Hell. The commentators report that when Abu Jahl and his companions heard of it they mocked, eating dates with butter and claiming it was the zaqqum, and this became a trial for the wrongdoers, as Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi state. The word talh means the fruit, which the Quran likens to the heads of devils; some take this to mean the devils themselves, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj describe ugly crested serpents, and others a known tree in Yemen, the comparison being imaginative since ugliness is fixed in the soul. The commentators agree that the people of the Fire are forced to eat from it until their bellies are full, then given a mixture of boiling water to drink, and afterward returned to Hell; they differ on the meaning of the return. The verses close by explaining this fate through blind imitation of forefathers in error, and through the sending of warners: the end of those who denied was destruction, except the sincere servants of God who were saved.

God states that the delights of Paradise promised to the believers are a better hospitality than the tree of zaqqum, the food of the people of the Fire. He made it a trial for the wrongdoers among the disbelievers, who found it absurd that a tree could grow in fire when fire consumes trees, and so they rejected it. The commentators describe the tree as springing from the bottom of Hell, and its fruit, called ṭalʿ, as hideous,

This verse describes the tree of zaqqum as one that grows at the root of the Blazing Fire, whose branches reach down through its levels, and whose fruit (talh) is hideous, like the heads of devils. The commentators explain that the damned will eat from it until their bellies are filled, then be given a scalding drink mixed with what they have eaten, and finally be returned to the Fire.

The commentators agree that the verse is set against the description of the delights of Paradise: just as the believers have a known provision, the wrongdoers have this tree as their food. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the Quraysh found this hard to believe, since fire burns trees, and that the verse became a trial (fitna) for the wrongdoers. According to these reports, Abu Jahl had dates and butter brought to his companions and told them it was the zaqqum. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi note that fitna can mean a test, a punishment, or a cause of doubt, depending on the opinion.

On the nature of the tree, the commentators differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi describe it as a bitter, repellent plant, and Qutrub holds that it grows in Tihama, while Ibn Atiyya links it to a poisonous plant of the arid lands. As for the image of the 'heads of devils', al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it as an image of ugliness grounded in what the mind imagines, citing al-Imru' al-Qays; others understand it as a crested serpent or a plant called al-Astan.

The commentators agree that shawb means a mixture, and that the scalding water is blended with what has been eaten. They differ, however, on the particle thumma: some take it as an order of narration, others as a sequence in time, and Ibn Kathir cites a reading in which the return to the Fire follows a passage outside it.

This verse describes the tree of zaqqum, which grows at the bottom of Hell, and sets it against the provision of the people of Paradise in a rhetorical question that invites comparison. The commentators explain that its fruit, the spathe, is hideous in appearance and taste, like the heads of devils, and that the damned are forced to eat it until their bellies are full, then given a scalding mixture of boiling water to drink on top of it, before returning to the Fire. The interpreters broadly agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid report that the Quraysh mocked the idea of a tree growing in fire, and that Abu Jahl ridiculed it with butter and dates; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold instead that zaqqum is a known tree of Tihama, and that fitna means a trial or a punishment. As for the phrase "like the heads of devils", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Qurazi take it as an imaginative image based on the ugliness people attribute to devils; al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir speak of maned serpents, while others such as Ibn 'Atiyya mention a shrub called al-Astan. Al-Zamakhshari combines these readings in an imaginative sense. Al-Razi explains the fitna as the doubt that seized the unbelievers, whereas al-Zajjaj understands it as a test. The commentators also differ on the particle "thumma" in "then their return": some see a real sequence in which the damned go out to drink the hamim before being sent back, others a purely narrative order. All agree that the verse warns the disbelievers and consoles the Prophet with the example of earlier peoples.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a comparison between the delights of the people of Paradise and the food of the people of the Fire. God asks which is better as a welcome gift, and then describes the tree of zaqqum as growing at the root of Hellfire, its blossoms hideous like the heads of devils. The disbelievers eat from it and fill their bellies. The exegetes agree that this eating comes from intense hunger or from being compelled. They are then given a drink of boiling water mixed with what they ate, and they return to the Fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the Quraysh doubted that a tree could grow in fire, and that Abu Jahl mocked the zaqqum by calling it dates and butter, so the verse became a trial for them. The commentators differ on the 'heads of the devils'. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as an image of the ugliness of devils as imagined in minds, though unseen; al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj take it as a serpent with a crest; others as a plant known in Yemen. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir allow that the tree may be a single tree whose branches reach throughout Hell, or a kind of tree. The word shawb means a mixture, read with a fatha or a damma. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand thumma as a rise in severity rather than a sequence in time. Ibn Kathir holds that the return to the Fire follows the drink, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan allow that the return may follow the meal. The verse closes with the blind imitation of forefathers in error and the salvation of God's sincere servants.

This passage from Surat As-Saffat describes the fate of the disbelievers in the Hereafter: they eat from the tree of al-Zaqqum, whose fruit is bitter, foul and repulsive, and they are forced to fill their bellies with it. They are then given a mixture of boiling water, the hamim, which is mixed with what is in their stomachs, and afterwards they are returned to Hell. The commentators agree that the verse concerns the punishment of the disbelievers, and that likening the spathe of the tree to the heads of devils expresses its extreme ugliness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that shawb means mixing and that hamim is extremely hot water, which mixes with the food in their bowels. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also report that the thirst drives them to drink this draught. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain the word "then" as marking a sequence of stages or an increase in torment. On the question of the return to the fire, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi hold that they are led out of Hell to drink the hamim and then brought back, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as their final abode. On the nature of the tree, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas link it to the episode in which Abu Jahl mocked the word zaqqum, whereas al-Mawardi reports that Qutrub took it to be a bitter tree of Tihama. All agree in condemning the blind imitation of forefathers in error, which al-Razi considers sufficient on its own to ground the rebuke.

This part of the verse describes the fate of the damned: after eating from the zaqqum tree they are given a scalding mixture to drink, and then they return to the Fire. The commentators differ on the meaning of the return. Ibn Zayd, Sufyan and Ibn Kathir take it as their final abode in Hell, while Muqatil, Yahya ibn Salam, Abu Hayyan and others hold that the boiling water lies outside the Fire, so that the damned are led to it as camels are led to water and then brought back to the blaze, citing the verse, 'they circulate between it and boiling water.' Al-Zamakhshari explains that 'then' (thumma) signals a gap in rank: the drink is worse than the food. Al-Tabari explains that the shawb means mixing, and that the boiling water is mixed into the food in the stomach. Some commentators say the mixture includes pus and fluids from the bodies of the damned. Ibn Mas'ud's reading 'their resting place' instead of 'their return' is noted as supporting the idea of an intermediate stage. All agree on the reason for this punishment: the damned blindly followed their fathers in error, hastening along their footsteps without examining the proof. This blind imitation is presented as the cause of what they endure.

The commentators explain that verse 69 of Surat As-Saffat gives the reason for the punishment of the idolaters: they found their fathers astray and hastened after them in their path without reflection or evidence. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya state that "alfaw" means "found" and that "yuhra'un" means "they hasten". Mujahid describes it as a running similar to a trot, al-Farra' as a hurry accompanied by a trembling, and Abu 'Ubayda as people being urged on from behind. All agree that the address concerns the Quraysh who rejected the call to monotheism and clung to the customs of their ancestors, and that the aim is to condemn blind imitation. Al-Razi says this verse alone would suffice to condemn taqlid. The differences concern context rather than meaning. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya link the verse to the return of the damned to the Blazing Fire and see it as the cause of their punishment, while al-Sha'rawi draws from the passive form of the verb that evil draws people more quickly than good. The central message stays the same: an inherited error does not excuse one who abandons evidence and reflection.

The commentators explain that the verse describes the fate of the disbelievers in Hell: after eating from the tree of Zaqqum and being forced to fill their bellies with it, they are given boiling water mixed into what they have eaten, and then they are sent back to the Blazing Fire. The phrase 'they hasten upon the traces of their fathers' means that they rush to follow their forefathers into error, the verb yuhra'un describing a hurried gait close to trembling, as Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd say. Al-Kalbi adds that they act as their fathers did, while Ibn Kathir sees in it a rebuke of blind imitation without proof.

The commentators agree that the verse refers to the Quraysh and those like them, and that following the fathers into error is the cause of the punishment they deserve. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'alfaw' means 'found'. Al-Razi holds that this verse alone would suffice to condemn blind imitation. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the fit between their offence, following without reflection, and their punishment, imposed without choice.

The particle 'thumma' marks, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, a delay between the state of the food and that of the drink, which is more severe. Opinions differ on 'marji'ahum': al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir take it as their final destination, whereas Yahya ibn Salam and Muqatil understand that they are led round between the boiling water and the Fire.

The commentators explain that the verse means most of the earlier nations had strayed from the path of truth before the Quraysh, and that God sent them warners to alert them to His punishment for their disbelief. They denied these messengers and rejected their advice, so God brought His chastisement upon them, and the Prophet and the listener are told to reflect on how those who were warned ended. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi read this as a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the Quraysh. The exception, 'except the sincere servants of God', refers to the believers who were saved, whom God chose for faith in Him and His messengers, as al-Tabari and al-Baghawi state. Al-Zamakhshari treats it as a connected exception, since the believers were among the warned yet did not share their fate. The word 'al-mukhlasin' is read in two ways: with a kasra, meaning those who made their worship sincere for God, or with a fatha, meaning those whom God chose, as al-Tabari, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi report. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi add that this straying came from blind imitation and neglect of reflection, and Ibn Sa'di notes that the believers were few. The commentators do not elaborate further, as the general meaning is broadly accepted.

This part of the verse states that God did not leave the earlier nations without warning: He sent among them messengers who alerted them to God's punishment if they persisted in disbelief. This is the apparent meaning on which the commentators agree. Al-Tabari explains that the prophets warned their peoples of God's might because of their unbelief; the peoples denied them and rejected their counsel, so God sent His punishment upon them. Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and Abu al-Su'ud take the same sense, adding that the messengers exposed the falsehood of what the people followed and warned them of its dreadful end. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand the warners as prophets who cautioned people about the consequences of their conduct. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi connect the verse with what precedes it, namely the misguidance of the fathers and the blind imitation of them; the warning then stands as proof against the people, who have no excuse once it has reached them. The commentators see in this verse a consolation for the Prophet and a threat to the Quraysh: what befell the earlier peoples could befall them too. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that the emphasis by oath is meant to give the message its full force. The differences concern mainly the details of the scenes described and the interpretation of the exception that follows, the sincere servants of God who were saved. As a whole, the verse establishes God's rule that messengers come before punishment, inviting the reader to reflect on the fate of the disbelievers and on that of the believers.

This verse asks the reader to consider the fate of those who were warned by their prophets yet rejected the message: their end was punishment and ruin. The commentators agree that the "warned ones" are the disbelievers who received the warning and did not accept it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the exception "except the sincere servants of God" refers to the monotheist believers who were saved. Al-Suddi adds that the "sincere" are those whom God chose for Himself. Al-Zamakhshari ties the meaning to the reading, either the servants' own sincerity or God's selection of them.

Most exegetes see the verse as both a consolation to the Prophet and a warning to the Quraysh, since many peoples went astray before them and God sent messengers to them. Al-Razi notes that the address "look" seems to be to the Prophet but in fact targets the unbelievers who had heard the accounts of the destroyed nations. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the looking may be physical or inward, and that the two can be combined without contradiction. Several commentators also point out that the phrase "how was the end" signals the severity of the punishment and its fitness to the sin.

The passage leads into the story of Noah, whom Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya present as the first messenger, and whose descendants alone remained after the flood. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that Noah's good name endured among later generations. As for the division of his sons among the peoples, the commentators relate it without treating it as certain; some cite Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, while others do not take this detail as established.

This passage explains that earlier nations went astray and that God sent warners to them to caution them against the consequences of disbelief, so their end was destruction. The commentators explain that the exception "except the sincere servants of God" refers to those who were saved from punishment because they believed and devoted their religion to God alone, or to those whom God chose and purified for His worship. The reading "al-mukhlaṣīn" with a fatḥa means God chose them, while "al-mukhliṣīn" with a kasra means they themselves were sincere. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi favour the sense of those God selected, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that both readings converge in meaning. On the scope of the exception, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir link it to the warned or to the misguided, while Ibn 'Ashur treats it as a connected exception, since these believers were among the warned but did not share their fate.

The passage then turns to the story of Noah: his prayer to God was answered, his people were drowned, he and his household were saved, and his offspring became the ones who remained. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that all people descend from Noah, while others note that his line was extended without asserting that all descend from him. The peace and praise granted to Noah are presented as a reward for his patience under the abuse of his people.

This verse recounts that Noah called upon his Lord, and that God answered him fully. After a long preaching that had only driven his people away, Noah prayed against the unbelievers, and God destroyed them by the flood while saving Noah and those who believed with him. The commentators read the call as a supplication and a plea for help, and the plural in 'the best of responders' as a plural of majesty. They agree that the great distress is the drowning, though al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya add the harm Noah suffered from his people. On descent, most, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, state that all people after Noah descend from him, through his three sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, while al-Zamakhshari notes that only his line remained once his companions in the ark had died. On 'We left him a good name among the later generations', Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take it as a lasting good reputation, whereas al-Kisa'i, al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari understand that the greeting 'Peace upon Noah' is itself what was left, repeated across the ages. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di draw a general rule that God rewards in this way every doer of good, and they describe Noah as a believing servate whose excellence lay in his faith and in his kindness to others.

This verse says that God rescued Noah and his family from the great distress. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Sudi, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, identify this distress as the flood and drowning, while Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also include the harm his people inflicted on him, and al-Alusi notes that both readings can be combined. The commentators understand 'his family' as those who believed with him, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that his wife and son were not saved, as other verses show, although the wording here is general. For the next verse, Ibn Abbas and Qatada say that all people after the flood descend from Noah, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi list the traditional division among Shem, Ham and Japheth and the peoples said to descend from each. Al-Qurtubi adds that others held that Noah's descendants were not limited to his three sons. On 'We left for him a good mention among the later generations', Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as a lasting good reputation, while al-Kisai, al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari read the phrase 'peace upon Noah' as a quoted saying that people will repeat. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see the whole passage as a reward for Noah's faith, patience and good conduct.

In this verse God mentions another favour granted to Noah after saving him and his household from the flood: his descendants were the ones who remained on earth once his people were destroyed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya agree that all people after the flood descend from Noah. They cite a hadith narrated by Samura about Noah's three sons, Sam, Ham and Japheth, from whom, respectively, the Arabs and Persians, the black peoples, and the Turks and Slavs are said to descend. Al-Zamakhshari repeats this division, and Ibn Abbas reports that everyone who was in the ark died after leaving it except his sons and their wives. Ibn Ashur judges that Noah's line continued among peoples who do not trace back to him, and that the flood may not have covered the entire earth, although he does not reject the universal scope of the verse. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy stress that the pronoun "they" implies exclusivity: only this line survived. Some commentators, including al-Qurtubi, note that others besides Noah's sons may have had descendants, and propose restricting the meaning to Noah's descendants and the believers who were with him. Ibn Kathir considers the hadith about the three sons sound, while other exegetes hold that it is not established, so these details remain a matter of debate among the commentators.

This passage from Surat as-Saffat states that God preserved for Noah, among the generations that followed, a lasting good name and praise until the Day of Resurrection, and that people greet him with peace and pray for him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others explain that "We left for him" means "We preserved for him a fine praise", and that the "tongue of truth" given to Noah is the praise uttered about him by the prophets and peoples, as reported from Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi. As for "Peace be upon Noah", most commentators take it as a greeting from God, a guarantee that no one would mention him with evil; al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari hold instead that the phrase is a quoted saying, meaning that God left this very phrase for him so that people would greet him with it until the last day, while al-Tabari regards the two meanings as close. God grounds this reward in Noah's goodness and in the fact that he was one of His believing servants; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that faith is the highest of praiseworthy qualities. On the phrase "those who remain", Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada hold that all people descend from Noah, and Ibn Kathir reports that his three sons were Sam, Ham and Japheth, the others having been drowned in the flood, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya are more cautious about these genealogical details. Ibn 'Ashur notes that describing the disbelieving peoples as "the others" carries a note of contempt, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi observe that the expression affirms the lasting continuity of good praise across all generations.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the account of Noah and means that God preserved for him a good reputation and lasting praise among the generations that would come after him until the Day of Judgment. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi understand the lasting praise as the reputation for truthfulness, and Mujahid calls it a tongue of truth given to all the prophets. Al-Tabari sees the greeting as a divine assurance that no one will speak ill of him. The Kufan grammarians, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari take the sentence as quoted speech, the object of the verb "We left", meaning that people greet him and pray for him from age to age. Others, such as Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi, treat it as a separate statement made by God. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that this disagreement is largely about wording, since both views accept that the prophets are greeted and praised. Ibn Kathir says that the reward for those who do good is a good name in proportion to their merit. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress that this reward is tied to faith, the highest of the qualities praised, as the next verse shows in calling Noah one of God's believing servants. Ibn Ashur adds that the many nations descended from Noah have all kept his memory with honour.

This verse states that God rewards the good-doers in the same way He rewarded Noah: He grants them a lasting good name among later generations and His peace upon them among all the worlds. The commentators explain that ihsan here means sincere faith, obedience and patience in the face of the people's harm. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi regard the lasting good name left to Noah as the reward itself, and read the sentence as explaining what God did for him. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the reward includes both the enduring remembrance and the greeting of peace offered to him by all the worlds. Al-Razi links these honours to Noah's ihsan and then explains that ihsan by his servanthood and faith. Some scholars, such as Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di, widen ihsan to cover good worship of God and kindness to creatures, while al-Qurtubi and others confine it to what relates to the reward described. All agree that faith is the highest quality praised. The verse ends by mentioning the drowning of the others, which confirms God's justice and power. The commentators agree on the general sense, but differ on how broad the meaning of ihsan should be.

This part of the verse says that Noah, peace be upon him, was one of Allah's believing servants, who affirmed Allah, declared Him one and devoted worship to Him sincerely. This faith is the reason for the salvation and good remembrance that Allah granted him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that faith is the highest quality of praise, and that linking his good deeds to faith shows its great value. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that God mentioned Noah's faith to encourage people toward it and to show that it is the highest rank of servants, so the praise of Noah is in fact praise of faith itself. Al-Tabari explains servanthood as Noah's affirmation of God's oneness and his worship of Him alone, while Ibn Kathir adds that believers are those who affirm and are certain. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as the justification for the good deeds that earned Noah his reward, and he notes that ascribing servanthood to Allah honours it. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi clarify that 'then We drowned the others' refers to the disbelievers of his people, since only the believers were saved in the ark. The commentators agree on this reading, and faith is the explicit cause stated in this verse.

This verse states that after saving Noah and those with him in the ark, God drowned the rest of his people, the "others," meaning the disbelievers who rejected him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that these are the unbelievers of Noah's people, none of whom survived. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the word "others" carries a tone of disdain toward them, as al-Sha'rawi also observes. Ibn 'Ashur reads the "then" (thumma) as indicating a difference in rank rather than time: destroying the disbelievers was a greater vindication of Noah than his mere rescue. Several commentators, including Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya, point out that the verse does not explicitly say the flood covered the whole earth. Some scholars hold that it did and conclude that all humanity descends from Noah, while others restrict the flood to his people. All agree on the lesson: the fate of this nation is a warning to unbelievers and a consolation to the Prophet.

This verse states that Abraham was among the followers of Noah, that is, among those who held his religion and followed his path, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, who take the pronoun to refer to Noah. Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi take it to refer to Muhammad, peace be upon him. The commentators agree that the word shi'a means followers and helpers, and that the 'sound heart' is one cleansed of polytheism, doubt and every fault of the heart; al-Hasan understood it as free from association with God, while 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr understood it as a heart that never curses.

The exegetes then describe how Abraham rebuked his father and his people for worshipping idols. He asked them what they worshipped, reproached them for serving false gods instead of God, and warned them of what awaited them before their Lord. Ibn Kathir and al-Biqa'i explain that these questions carry the force of denunciation and disapproval. On the grammar of the word ifkan, al-Zamakhshari took it as an object of purpose, while others took it as a direct object or a circumstantial complement.

The later commentaries dwell on the episode of the stars and the sickness. Most hold that Abraham used an ambiguous statement when he said he was sick; al-Hasan saw it as a reflection on what he would do, and al-Dahhak saw it as a prediction that he would fall ill with the sickness of death. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that lying is not permitted to prophets and that these words are read as indirect speech. The commentaries then describe the breaking of the idols, the sentence to be thrown into the fire, and God's protection of him from it.

These verses tell the story of Abraham and his stand against his people. The commentators explain that "the faction of Noah" refers to those who followed his religion, path and creed, and that Abraham was among them. As for "a sound heart", Qatada, Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take it to mean a heart free from polytheism and doubt, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr says it means one that never curses, and Ibn Sirin says it means knowing that God is true and that the Hour is coming. Others understand it as freedom from all the diseases of the heart, such as envy, spite and arrogance. Abraham rebuked his father and his people for worshipping idols, asking them in a tone of reproach what they worship, and the commentators describe these gods as a lie, the worst of lies, warning them against their audacity toward the Lord of the worlds. All agree that he broke their idols after they had gone out to their festival, but they differ over his words "I am sick". Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it as a hint of a contagious illness such as plague, al-Dahhak as a future deadly illness, al-Hasan as a reflection on what to do, while some see it as an equivocation. Ibn Kathir and others cite the hadith about the three lies, which indicates he was not truly sick. On the identity of the sacrificed son mentioned later, most commentators name Isaac, while Ibn Kathir favours Ishmael, and no single view is settled among them.

The commentators explain that this verse records Ibrahim, peace be upon him, rebuking his father and his people with a question of censure: "What is it that you worship?" The phrase "Is it a fabrication, gods other than God, that you desire?" means that they seek false deities apart from God. Most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, hold that the pronoun in "his party" refers to Nuh, and that Ibrahim followed him in the core of monotheism even though their laws differed; al-Farra' and al-Kalbi instead take it to refer to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. As for "a sound heart", Qatada understood it as free from doubt, al-Hasan as free from associating partners with God, al-Dahhak as sincere, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr as never cursing, and al-Razi widened it to cover every stain on the heart such as hatred and envy.

The words "What then do you think of the Lord of the worlds?" are a warning and a reproach: what do you imagine He will do to you when you worship another besides Him? Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi adopt this reading. All agree that the question is one of rebuke and denial. Grammarians differ over the role of "fabrication": al-Zamakhshari treats it as an object of purpose, others as an object or a circumstantial phrase, and al-Tabari does not settle the matter.

The tafsir literature links this passage to the episode in which Ibrahim looks at the stars and says "I am sick". Ibn 'Abbas explains that he wanted to excuse himself from his people's festival, al-Dahhak that he was announcing a future illness, and al-Hasan that he was reflecting on what to do. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard this as an allusive expression rather than a literal lie, while al-Razi offers several different explanations.

This verse records Abraham's words to his father and people rebuking them for worshipping idols: do you desire fabricated gods, lies, apart from God? The commentators explain that 'ifk' means falsehood, and that it is the worst kind of lie. On grammar, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan give several readings: 'ifkan' as an object of purpose with 'alihatan' as the direct object, or 'ifkan' as the direct object with 'alihatan' in apposition, or as a circumstantial state meaning 'lying'. Most favour the first. The question carries reproach and rebuke, and the next line, 'What then is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?', is a warning: what do you think He will do to you when you meet Him after worshipping another? Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy also cite Qatada, who reads it as a warning against associating partners with God. Ibn Ashur explains that 'zann' here means a mistaken belief, and that its object may imply an attribute of lordship or the very nature of the Lord. The exegetes conclude that the verse confronts Abraham's people with what they already acknowledge: God is the Lord of the worlds, so why do they associate others with Him?

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the account of Abraham and his people. It is a rhetorical question of rebuke and warning: what do you think the Lord of the worlds will do with you when you meet Him after worshipping others besides Him? The general sense is that one who worships other than God cannot expect to go unpunished, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada state. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Biqa'i instead see it as a reminder of God's greatness and of the blessings He has bestowed on them. Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi read it as a warning against a wrong opinion of God, while al-Zamakhshari holds that you have conceived of God an image that has led you to associate others with Him. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the condemnation of idol worship, and Ibn Sa'di sees in it a warning of punishment for persisting in associationism. All agree that the word 'zann' here means a belief that does not match reality. The following verses about the destruction of the idols are generally read as continuing this passage. Regarding Abraham's words 'I am sick', al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report the views of Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak that he referred to a contagious illness such as plague, that of al-Hasan that it was a real illness, and others that it was a prediction, while al-Razi offers several further interpretations. Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abraham's three lies, and Ibn Kathir emphasises that this hadith underpins the reading of the phrase as an allusion. As for the word 'shi'a', Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean the followers of the same religion, while al-Farra' takes it to mean the followers of Muhammad.

The commentators explain that when Abraham's people invited him to join their festival, he looked at the stars and declared that he was sick. They then left him and went off. Most agree that gazing at the stars was a habit of his astrologer people, and that he thereby led them to think he was reading a sign of illness to come. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the sickness was understood as plague, which his people greatly feared, and that the statement was an equivocation rather than an outright lie. Qatada notes that Arabs say of someone who reflects that he has 'looked at the stars', meaning he is pondering his matter, while al-Hasan takes the word to mean what presented itself to him as a course of action. Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab relate that he had seen a rising star linked with plague, and Ibn Zayd that a particular star accompanied each of his illnesses. As for 'I am sick', al-Dahhak reads it as 'I will become sick', others as sickness of heart at their disbelief, and Ibn Ashur as a pretext to remain alone with the idols. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy discuss the hadith of Abraham's three lies, with al-Razi holding that it cannot be taken literally and Ibn Juzayy offering several readings. Al-Zamakhshari allows such equivocation in cases of necessity. All agree on what follows: left alone, he smashed the idols with his right hand, and when questioned he confronted them with their helplessness, after which they resolved to burn him, but God saved him and turned their plot against them.

Al-Tabari and other commentators report that when Ibrahim's people invited him to join their festival, he looked at the stars and said he was sick, so they left him behind. The commentators differ on the meaning of the look and the sickness. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Zayd say that a rising star signalled an illness, perhaps plague, which his people feared, so he used the excuse of sickness to stay. Al-Hasan and Qatada understand the look as reflection on a plan, while al-Dahhak explains the word as meaning he would soon fall ill. All agree that he stayed alone to deal with the idols: after the people left, he smashed them with his right hand. When they returned and found the damage, they questioned him, he confronted them with their error, and they then resolved to throw him into a fire from which God saved him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir describe his words as an indirect statement rather than an outright lie, and some discuss the hadith about Ibrahim's three lies, reading it as a figure of speech. Some take the sickness to mean a sickness of heart at their disbelief. All stress that his heart was sound, free of idolatry and doubt. The verse also argues that God created people and their works, so worshipping what people shape is absurd. Opinions on astrology divide the commentators: some reject it, while others accept observing the stars for direction and timekeeping without believing they govern events.

God tells of Abraham, peace be upon him, who asked his people what they worshipped and urged them to consider what they thought of the Lord of the worlds. He then looked at the stars and said he was sick, so his people turned away from him and went to their festival, leaving the temple of the idols open to him. The commentators agree that "they turned away from him, retreating" means they left him and went off, and that "I am sick" was an excuse for not joining them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the sickness may have been plague, whose contagion they feared, while al-Dahhak takes it as a sickness yet to come, and al-Hasan says he was reflecting on what to do. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that his gazing at the stars concerned the astral science his people practised, which he used to make his point, and that the words were a veiled remark rather than a plain lie, though some cite the hadith of the three lies and explain it as a figure of speech. Most exegetes say he struck the idols with his right hand, which Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi understand as strength or as the oath he had earlier sworn. All report that his people then wanted to burn him, but God made the fire cool and safe for him, so that his opponents were the ones humbled.

This passage of Surat as-Saffat describes Abraham's stratagem against his people. He slipped away to their idols, before which food had been placed for blessing, and mocked them: 'Will you not eat? Why do you not speak?' Then he struck them with his right hand and smashed them. The commentators agree that 'rāgha' means to turn aside secretly, and that the mockery highlights the idols' powerlessness. On his words 'I am sick', which excused him from the festival, they differ. Ibn Abbas and those who follow him take it as a reference to plague, which the people were fleeing; Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Sufyan take it as an infectious illness, namely plague; Qatada reads 'he looked at the stars' as an idiom for reflection; al-Hasan takes it as deliberation over what to do; Ibn Zayd reports that the star rising was linked to his sickness; al-Dahhak says he would fall ill with the sickness of death. Ibn Kathir and others treat these words as indirect speech (ma'arid), not a blameworthy lie, citing the authentic hadith that Abraham lied only three times, while noting that this is not a real lie. Al-Razi and others reject the idea that he practised astrology and explain the gazing as reflection. On who 'his party' refers to, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say Noah, while al-Farra' says Muhammad. All agree that the idols were smashed after the people returned from their festival, and that they then inquired who had done it.

This passage recounts how Abraham, wishing to show his people that their idols were powerless, seized the moment when they left for a festival. Having left food before the idols, he mocked them: 'Will you not eat? What is wrong with you that you do not speak?' He then struck them with his right hand, as most commentators explain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that this was ironic mockery meant to expose that these objects neither eat nor speak. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read 'with the right hand' as the stronger hand, or as force, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention that it may refer to the oath he had sworn earlier. The phrase 'I am sick' (saqim) is read in several ways: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take it as an allusive or evasive remark, whereas others understood it as the plague, which the people fled, allowing him to remain behind. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan cite the hadith of Abraham's three 'lies' and explain that these were ambiguous statements rather than real falsehoods, though al-Razi questions the chain of transmission. On the verb yazuffun, al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy link it to hastening, while Abu Hayyan notes several readings. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi draw from the end of the verse that human actions are created by God, a view other commentators do not share. All agree on the outcome: after Abraham's argument, the people decided to throw him into the fire, but God made it cool and safe for him, and their scheme turned against them.

The commentators explain that when the idols were left alone during the people's festival, Abraham went secretly to them and struck them with force using his right hand, smashing them to pieces. Earlier he had mocked them by offering them food and asking why they did not speak. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi, take «bil-yamin» literally as the right hand, which is the stronger, or figuratively as strength, a view also held by al-Farra' and Tha'lab. Ibn Juzayy, al-Zamakhshari and others add that it may refer to the oath Abraham had sworn earlier, «By God, I will surely plot against your idols», so the blow was carried out because of that oath. Al-Qurtubi mentions a reading that links the right hand to justice, but presents it as a distant meaning. The verb «faraagha» means to turn aside stealthily or to come upon them; Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a sly approach to the idols. On «yazIfoon», the majority read the verb as a rapid walk or run, while Hamza reads it in the causative form, meaning to drive others to hasten; the commentators agree on the general sense of haste. When the people learned what had happened they rushed to Abraham, who answered by rebuking them for worshipping what they carve themselves, while God created them and their deeds. Commentators differ on whether «ma» is a verbal noun or a relative pronoun, and Sunni scholars cite the verse as proof that human actions are created by God. Unable to answer his argument, the people turned to force, ordering a great furnace built into which they cast him, but God made them the humiliated losers.

This verse describes the people of Abraham rushing toward him after learning that he had smashed their idols. The commentators agree on the general sense of the verb yazuffun, but differ on its nuance. The majority, including Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, understand it as hurrying, and al-Zamakhshari, followed by Ibn 'Atiyya, links it to the first running stride of the ostrich. Al-Suddi and another report from Qatada take it to mean walking, Mujahid sees a proud gait, al-Dahhak understands running, and Yahya ibn Sallam explains it as trembling with anger. Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud report that when they returned from their festival and found the idols broken, they asked who had done it, suspected Abraham, and came to him in haste. Al-Tabari notes that the reading with an open initial vowel is the best known among the Arabs, while the reading with a closed initial vowel is attributed to Hamza and al-A'mash, and some rarer readings exist. These differences do not change the central meaning: the people come to call him to account, which prepares the debate that follows.

This verse records Abraham's rebuke to his people after he had smashed their idols: 'Do you worship what you carve?' The commentators agree that it reproaches people for worshipping what their own hands have made, and that the question is one of disapproval. The disagreement concerns the particle 'mā' in the following clause, 'and God created you and what you make'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a verbal noun, meaning 'God created you and your work', and they take this as proof that human actions are created by God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan read it as a relative pronoun, 'what you carve', meaning the idols themselves; Ibn al-Qayyim argues this gives a stronger proof against them. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the verbal-noun reading disrupts the structure of the verse. Other scholars suggest a negative or interrogative reading, which Ibn Juzayy considers wrong. Ibn 'Ashur highlights the tone of challenge and logical argument. The main lesson drawn by the commentators is that a god worthy of worship must be the Creator, not a creature.

This passage from Surat al-Saffat tells the story of Ibrahim, who belonged to the same line of faith as Nuh and came to his Lord with a sound heart free of association. He denounced to his father and people their worship of idols, then pretended to be ill to avoid joining their festival. When the temple was empty, he smashed the idols with his right hand and great force. On their return, when they confronted him, he asked whether they worship what they carve with their own hands, when God created them and what they make. The commentators agree that this verse serves as an argument against idol worship, since the idols themselves are God's creation. They differ on the grammar of the word 'ma' in 'what you make'. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a relative pronoun, meaning that God created the idols you shape, while Ibn Qayyim, al-Suhayli and Ibn Qutayba read it as a verbal noun meaning 'your work', in line with the Sunni view that God creates human acts; al-Zamakhshari judged that this reading weakens the argument. As for the right hand, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' took it as strength, others as the hand itself, and others as the oath Ibrahim had sworn earlier. Hamza read the verb with a different vowel from the majority, which gives the sense of hastening. Al-Razi concludes that the verse shows that human actions are created by God while being acquired by people, a position Ibn Uthaymin also upholds.

This verse tells that after Abraham had defeated his people with argument and exposed the worthlessness of their idols, they turned to force. They ordered a great structure to be built, filled with wood, set alight, and Abraham thrown into the blaze. The commentators agree that al-Jahim means a fire of intense blaze, and that the plot they intended was to burn him. God made them the lowest, that is, defeated and humiliated, by saving him from the fire and frustrating their scheme. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that God made the fire cool and safe for Abraham. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that most scholars understand Abraham's words 'I am going to my Lord' as his migration to Syria, while Qatada takes it as a departure of heart and intention, and others link it to the moment they wanted to cast him into the fire. On the structure, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil describe a tall wall of stone or iron, while others say it was a catapult. Ibn Ashur explains that al-Jahim is a fire upon fire, an ember upon an ember. The commentators do not settle the details of the construction and remain with the Qur'anic brevity.

This verse reports that Abraham's people, having been defeated by his argument, plotted to burn him, but God foiled their scheme and made them the lowest, meaning the defeated and humiliated. The commentators agree on the plain sense: their plan to cast him into the fire rebounded on them, for God saved him from the flames. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the kayd was the burning they had prepared, and that al-Asfalin are the losers or the vanquished. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and the Jalalayn see the words as humiliation and defeat, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the defeat had already taken place in the debate, as well as in the fire. Al-Tabari and Qatada report that Abraham did not argue with them again until they were destroyed. Several works, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, describe the building in which he was to be thrown, and some say it was a catapult; none settles the matter decisively. The commentators report that the fire became cool and safe for him, as the verse in al-Anbiya indicates. Ibn 'Ashur notes that asfalin here means the vanquished, whereas akhsirin in al-Anbiya means those whose effort yields nothing. Ibn 'Uthaymin explains that kayd is seeking to harm an opponent without his noticing. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that their pride made them think they had the upper hand before the tables turned. Most read in the passage the helplessness of the deniers before God's power and the protection He grants the believer.

After God had saved Ibrahim from his people's plot and he had come out of the fire unharmed, he declares that he is going to his Lord, meaning he will emigrate from his homeland to a place where he can worship God freely, trusting that God will guide him to what is good for his religion and his life. The commentators differ on when he spoke these words. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi place them after his escape from the fire, when he resolved to migrate toward Syria. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report another view, attributed to Qatada and Sulayman ibn Surad, that he said them before being thrown into the fire, meaning he goes toward what God has decreed, even toward death and Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand guidance as steadfastness in the truth and divine support. Ibrahim then asks his Lord for a righteous son. Al-Tabari, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir report that he was granted a patient, forbearing boy. Most commentators identify this son as Isma'il, although the identity of the sacrificed son is disputed between Isma'il and Isaac. Al-Tabari and several early scholars favor Isaac, while Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur favor Isma'il, relying on the context of the verses and on reports attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the word gift is mostly used for a son. The Quran then tells that God ransomed the boy with a great sacrifice, that father and son both submitted to God's command, that He left Ibrahim a good name among later generations, and that He blessed him and Isaac, so that among their descendants there were both the righteous and those who wronged themselves.

The commentators explain that Abraham, after being saved from the fire and having silenced his people with argument, said, 'I am going to my Lord', meaning he would emigrate from his people's land to the place God had commanded, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari identify as Syria. Qatada understood it as going with the heart, intention and deeds, while Ibn Ashur saw it as an emigration to worship God free from trial. He then asked his Lord for a righteous son who would help him in his call and keep him company in exile. Al-Tabari notes that the word 'gift' is mainly used for a child, and al-Zamakhshari adds that it is also used of a brother in the verse about Aaron. The exegetes agree that God answered him with the news of a patient boy, and Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin explain 'halim' as patience and largeness of heart. On the identity of the promised son, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan hold it was Isma'il, while al-Tabari, al-Razi and others hold it was Isaac. Ibn Kathir considers the evidence for Isma'il stronger, whereas al-Razi leaves the question open, and Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi likewise note the disagreement without settling it. The general meaning remains a prayer for a righteous offspring, made by prophets with great hope for the reform of their descendants.

The commentators explain that after Abraham's prayer for a righteous son, God gives him the good news of a boy endowed with halim, that is forbearance, self-control and a patient, measured temper that shows itself as he grows. The exegetes agree that this glad tidings was given in answer to Abraham's supplication. On the identity of the son Abraham was commanded to sacrifice, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatada and 'Ikrima held it was Isaac, while Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi held it was Ishmael. Those who favour Isaac point out that his birth announcement is linked with Jacob's, while those who favour Ishmael note that the announcement of Isaac comes after the account of the sacrifice, and point to the ram's horns hung in the Ka'ba. Ibn Kathir inclines to Ishmael, al-Tabari to Isaac. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi stress that the glad tidings include childhood, maturity and gentleness of character. On the sacrifice itself, the commentaries report that Abraham saw in a dream that he was slaughtering his son, told him, the son accepted with patience, and God ransomed the boy with a great sacrifice, since the dreams of prophets are revelation. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'aslama' (submitting or surrendering) and on the grammar of the clause introduced by 'lamma'. They agree in praising Abraham and his descendants, and in recognising that God placed prophethood in his line.

The commentators relate that after Abraham was given the good news of a patient boy, the son grew to the age of walking with him. Abraham saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him and put the matter to him; the son answered with submission and patience, seeking God's pleasure. The ransom was a great ram, and God left Abraham a good name among later generations. The exegetes see in this trial the proof of the sincerity and obedience of the Friend of God, and hold that a prophet's dream is revelation. On who the sacrificed son was, opinions differ. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatada and al-Zuhri say it was Isaac, a view also reported from Ibn Abbas in one version. Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and al-Kalbi say it was Ishmael, relying on the order of the verses, where the good news of Isaac comes after the account of the sacrifice, and on the place of sacrifice in Mecca attested by the ram's horns hung at the Ka'ba. Al-Zajjaj concluded that God alone knows which it was. Ibn Jarir favoured Isaac, Ibn Kathir Ishmael, and each side supports its view with competing arguments. All agree on the son's remarkable patience, and that God followed the trial with peace and reward for the good-doers.

The commentators explain that "when they had both submitted" means they surrendered and yielded to God's command: Abraham prepared to slaughter his son, and the youth submitted to his father in what he had been told by his Lord. "And he laid him down on his brow" means he threw him down on his side until his forehead touched the ground. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the father laid him on his face or side, and cite the youth's words to his father transmitted through Mujahid and Ikrima. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi that the blade did not cut the throat, which they treat as something beyond ordinary perception. Ash-Sha'bi, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr state that the ransom was a ram. The commentators disagree on whether the sacrificed son was Isaac or Ishmael: Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Abbas favour Isaac, while Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas in one report, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, ash-Sha'bi and Mujahid favour Ishmael, relying on the promise of Isaac mentioned only after the sacrifice story and on a Bedouin's words to the Prophet calling him the son of the two sacrificed ones. Al-Zajjaj leaves the matter to God. Finally, scholars differ on whether a command may be abrogated before it is carried out: the Sunni scholars permit it, while the Mu'tazilites and some jurists deny it.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the moment God calls out to Abraham after he and his son had submitted to the command and Abraham had laid the boy down for sacrifice. God tells him: O Abraham, you have fulfilled what you saw in the dream, through your resolve and by giving everything in your power. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take this call as the realization of the vision rather than necessarily the completion of the slaughter. Al-Qurtubi reports that the Sunni scholars hold that the slaughter itself did not take place and that the command was abrogated before it was carried out, while others, such as al-Suddi, say God placed a copper plate on his throat, and al-Tabari and others report that the knife would not cut. The phrase 'Thus do We reward the good-doers' means that God frees the righteous from trials, as He freed Abraham. On the identity of the son, scholars differ: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Said ibn al-Musayyab say it was Ishmael, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy support this by noting that the promise of Isaac comes after the story of the sacrifice. Others, including Umar, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, say it was Isaac, while al-Zajjaj says that God alone knows. The passage closes with praise of Abraham, whose remembrance God leaves among later generations, with blessings upon him and Isaac, and with the distinction between descendants who do good and those who wrong themselves.

The commentators explain that God called out to Abraham after he and his son had submitted to the command and he had laid the boy on his brow ready for the sacrifice. He was told that he had fulfilled what he had seen in the dream, through his firm resolve and by doing everything within his power as preparation for the slaughter. They agree that the verse praises obedience and submission, and that the reward for the doers of good is the lifting of the trial. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the vision to have been fulfilled through the resolve and the readiness, while al-Qurtubi holds that the slaughter never took place, since the ransom came before the act, which amounts to abrogation before execution. Most read the phrase about the manifest trial as an evident test, but Ibn Zayd takes it to mean a blessing. The ransom was a great sacrifice: some say it came from paradise, others that it was an ordinary ram, and the scholars do not settle the matter. On the identity of the son, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi name Ishmael, while Ibn Mas'ud, Ali, Umar, al-Abbas, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Qatada name Isaac; al-Zajjaj declines to decide. As for the lasting praise left among later generations and the peace upon Abraham, the commentators read it as a good name God preserved for him among the peoples who came after.

This verse states that the command to sacrifice Abraham's son was a clear and severe test. The commentators explain the word 'trial' (bala') as an evident examination; al-Tabari reports Ibn Zayd's view that here it means harm rather than a test, while Muqatil reads it as a plain blessing, since God ransomed the son with a ram. The commentators agree that the scene follows the submission of father and son to God's command, and that this submission is itself the heart of the test. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi note that a command given by God becomes obedience, and that a trial may concern what a person does with his own hands, which is harsher. All agree on the ransom by a great ram, but differ on its origin: Ibn Abbas says it had grazed in Paradise, while al-Hasan says it was a mountain goat descended from Thabir.

On the identity of the son, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid hold it was Ishmael, relying on the Prophet's saying 'I am the son of the two sacrificed ones' and on the fact that the promise of Isaac is mentioned after the account of the sacrifice. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Abbas, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Qatada hold it was Isaac, relying on the promise given to Isaac and then Jacob. Ibn Kathir considers the view favouring Isaac to lack support in the Quran or Sunna and judges Ishmael the sounder opinion, while al-Zajjaj states that God alone knows which of the two was sacrificed. These differences do not establish any particular legal ruling.

God ransomed the son with a great sacrifice, after Abraham and his son had submitted fully to the command. The plain meaning is that a ram was substituted for the boy; commentators describe it as large in body or great in worth because it served as ransom for a prophet and the son of a prophet, which is the origin of the sacrifice tradition of the Eid. The commentators disagree on who was ransomed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid and al-Hasan say it was Isma'il, citing the hadith in which the Prophet calls himself son of the two sacrificed ones, the fact that the good news of Isaac comes after the account of the sacrifice, and the attributes of patience and fidelity to promise given to Isma'il. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Abbas and several followers such as Qatada, Ikrima and al-Zuhri say it was Isaac, relying on the promise of Isaac and then Jacob. Al-Tabari leans toward Isaac, Ibn Kathir toward Isma'il, and al-Zajjaj declines to decide. About the ram, some say it came from paradise and grazed there for forty years, others that it was the offering of Habil, and others that it was a wild goat. Greatness is explained as being accepted by God, as great in value, or as large in body. From this passage comes the view that the ransom by an animal makes the ordinary sacrifice lawful, and Abu Hanifa derives from it that a vow to slaughter one's son requires slaughtering a sheep.

This verse belongs to the story of the sacrifice in Surat as-Saffat. The commentators explain that God left Abraham a good name and a lasting praise among the peoples who would come after him until the Day of Judgment, and this is shown by the greeting that follows: 'Peace be upon Abraham.' Most agree that the 'leaving' concerns the good reputation. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that what is left is the greeting itself, or the greeting together with the good name. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the meaning as a good name that endures to the Last Day. Al-Mawardi reports two views: the good name, from Qatada, and the greeting, from Ikrima. Al-Tabari links this reward to Abraham's patience in obeying his Lord's command. The verse confirms that Abraham's elevated status is tied to his faith and his good deeds. The commentators agree that whenever his name is mentioned, a greeting of peace is offered to him.

The commentators explain that the verse "Peace be upon Abraham" is a greeting from God to His friend after He had delivered him from the trial and ransomed his son with a great sacrifice. It is an enduring praise and a preservation from every flaw, and several, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur, state that he will be mentioned by later generations only in goodness. Al-Tabari takes the verb "to leave" to mean "to preserve", with the fine praise as its object, while Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi consider that the sentence itself is what is left, meaning that the peace upon him is recited and invoked. The scholars differ on the identity of the son who was to be sacrificed. Most of the Companions and Successors, including Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Qatada, say it was Isaac, relying on the account of Jacob and on certain reports. Others, including Ibn Abbas in one of his transmissions, Ibn Umar, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, hold that it was Ishmael, citing the promise of Isaac mentioned after the story and the hadith "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones". Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim favour the view of Ishmael, al-Tabari that of Isaac, and al-Zajjaj leaves the matter to God's knowledge. As for the great sacrifice, some describe it as a ram from Paradise that had grazed there for forty years, others as a white ram with curved horns, others as a wild goat descended from Thabir, and some explain that it was called great because it was accepted by God.

The commentators explain that this verse, 37:110, closes the list of favours Allah bestowed on Abraham after ransoming his son with a great sacrifice. It states that Allah rewards the good-doers just as He rewarded Abraham for his obedience and his excellent submission to God's command. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand this as deliverance from hardship after trial together with lasting praise. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the sentence omits the emphatic 'inna' because the earlier passage already used it, and that repeating the phrase stresses the importance of rewarding the one who does good. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the reward includes deliverance from trials in this life and the next, while at-Tabari says that doing good covers both worship of God and good dealing with people. On the identity of the son, at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour Isma'il, whereas many companions and early scholars held that it was Isaac; ar-Razi sets out the arguments for both views without deciding. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi do not decide on this verse itself. The verse therefore belongs to the praise of Abraham and the blessing on his descendants, among whom are both the doer of good and the one who wrongs himself.

This verse affirms that Abraham was among Allah's believing servants.
