The commentators explain that God ransomed the boy whom Abraham had been ordered to sacrifice with a great sacrifice, left him a lasting good mention among later generations, and greeted him with peace. The exegetes differ on who the boy was. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Umar, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatada and al-Hasan, among others, say it was Isaac, relying on the promise of Isaac and then Jacob, and on a letter attributed to Jacob calling Isaac the sacrificed one of God. Ibn Abbas in one report, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and al-Hasan in one report, say it was Ishmael, arguing that the Quran describes him as patient, true to his promise and gentle, that the ram's horns were hung in the Kaaba, and that the promise of Isaac comes after the sacrifice story. Al-Tabari favours Isaac, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim favour Ishmael, each giving reasons. As for the ram, most describe a white horned ram tied to a thornbush at Thabir, though some report it had grazed in Paradise for forty years. Ibn Kathir regards many of these accounts as drawn from Jewish and Christian sources and unproven, and many scholars keep to the apparent sense of the verses.

The commentators explain that God gave Abraham the good news of Isaac, a prophet among the righteous, as a reward for his gratitude, obedience and patience. Ibn 'Abbas, through 'Ikrima, said the glad tidings came twice: once at Isaac's birth and once at his prophethood, while Qatada held that the prophethood was announced after Abraham was tested by the command to sacrifice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that the one sacrificed was Isma'il and that this annunciation of Isaac is separate, relying on the order of the narrative and on the later announcement of Ya'qub, which would contradict an order to slaughter Isaac. Others, including Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar and many Successors such as Qatada and Malik, say the sacrificed son was Isaac; Ibn Kathir considered this view to rest on reports from the People of the Book. The commentators also note the blessing granted to Abraham and Isaac through many descendants and the presence of most prophets among them. They add that their offspring includes both the virtuous believer and the one who wrongs himself by disbelief, so kinship with the prophets alone does not suffice.

The commentators explain that the verse "We blessed him and Isaac" means that God poured blessings upon Abraham and Isaac, including abundant offspring, and that most of the prophets came from their line. Among their descendants are "one who does good", meaning a believer obedient to God, and "one who clearly wrongs himself", meaning an unbeliever or a manifest sinner. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi draw the lesson that a person is judged by his own deeds rather than by his origin, for a righteous man may father a wicked son and a wicked man a righteous one. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir specify that the good-doer is the obedient one and the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever or the rebel. The verse is read by Ibn Kathir and others as praise of the Friend of God. The preceding verses concern the sacrifice, on which opinions differ. The majority of Companions and Successors, including Umar, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, held that the one to be sacrificed was Isaac, while Ibn Abbas in one transmission, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi held it was Ishmael. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi favour Ishmael, citing the Quranic context and the Torah's reference to the only son, while al-Tabari favours Isaac and al-Suyuti withholds judgment. Al-Razi and others discuss whether the command was abrogated before it was carried out, and the position that it was abrogated before execution is noted.

The commentators explain that God favoured Moses and Aaron, the sons of Imran, by granting them prophethood and the mission, and that He rescued them and their people from the great distress. Most identify this distress as the enslavement and humiliation imposed by Pharaoh on the Children of Israel, while some see it as the drowning that destroyed Pharaoh and his people. All agree that God gave them victory so that they became the dominant ones, and that He gave Moses the clear Book, the Torah, and guided them to the straight path, which Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy identify as Islam. God also left them a lasting good reputation among later generations, which is why peace is invoked upon them. The commentators differ over the pronoun in 'and We helped them': al-Farra', Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and most others take it to refer to Moses, Aaron and their people, since the context groups them together, whereas some grammarians take it to refer to the two brothers alone, out of honour, a view Ibn Juzayy considers weak. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the favour to be the prophethood and the rank that comes with it. On the 'great distress', al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy mention drowning or Pharaoh's domination, while al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur include the enslavement that preceded the sea. Ibn Sa'di and al-Baghawi stress that the peace upon them is an enduring praise, and that faith and good conduct are the reason for this reward.

This verse recalls God's favour upon Moses and Aaron and upon their people, the Children of Israel, in delivering them from the great distress. The commentators differ on what this distress was. Most, including Qatada, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn, Ibn Juzayy, al-Shawkani and al-Qasimi, understand it as the oppression and enslavement the Israelites suffered under Pharaoh and his people, including the slaughter of their sons and the sparing of their women. Al-Sudi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others take it to mean the drowning of Pharaoh and his people. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi mention both meanings, while Abu al-Su'ud favours enslavement and considers drowning unlikely since it was not a distress for the Israelites. Ibn 'Ashur includes the humiliation under the pharaohs and the fear of the army when it caught up with them at the sea, before the sea split for them. In the phrase 'and We made them victorious', most take the pronoun to refer to Moses, Aaron and their people, while a grammatical opinion, reported by al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan, limits it to the two prophets out of reverence. All agree that the Clear Book is the Torah and that the straight path is Islam or God's upright religion. Finally, the repeated greeting of peace upon Moses and Aaron is understood by Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim as a lasting good praise they retain among later generations, while al-Razi also considers that the Muslim community is meant to be the one sending them greetings.

This verse states that God granted victory to Moses, Aaron and their people over Pharaoh and his folk, so that they became the victors. Commentators explain that the pronoun in "We gave them victory" refers to Moses, Aaron and their people. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir accept this reading, while al-Farra' and Ibn Juzayy note that some scholars take it to refer to the two brothers alone, the plural being used to honour them, as the Arabs do with a leader and his followers. All agree that this victory followed a long period of humiliation, when Pharaoh's people enslaved the Children of Israel and killed their sons. Al-Tabari, al-Samarqandi and Ibn Kathir add that the victory was lasting, since God made the Children of Israel inherit the land of their oppressors. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the word "hum" is a pronoun of separation that implies restriction: they vanquished others but were never defeated, even though a victor may suffer setbacks in some battles. Al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi stress that Pharaoh's defeat was a complete destruction rather than a mere military loss. The disagreements thus concern the referent of the pronoun and the scope of the expression, not the general meaning of the verse.

This part of the verse recalls the favour God showed Moses and Aaron by giving them the clear Book, which the commentators agree is the Torah, described as explicit and detailed in its guidance and rulings, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Jalalayn note. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, identifies the straight path with Islam, the religion God sent through all His prophets, a view al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy share. Al-Razi reads the guidance more broadly, as the direction of reason and revelation, divine support and protection from error.

The commentators agree that the phrase about leaving them a good name among later generations means a lasting, honourable praise, and that the greeting of peace upon Moses and Aaron is part of it. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir see the closing formula as confirming that the believers are the ones who do good.

They differ on who is meant by the pronoun in the phrase about being granted victory. Al-Farra' and al-Qurtubi say it refers to Moses and Aaron alone, using the plural for honour, but al-Qurtubi considers it more correct that it includes their people, since the previous clause mentions them together. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir also present the collective reading. As for the great distress, Qatada and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to be Pharaoh's enslavement of the Israelites, al-Suddi, al-Razi and al-Tabari take it to be the drowning, and Ibn 'Atiyya combines both episodes. Al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani mainly hold the oppression view, and al-Shawkani treats it as the stronger reading.

This verse speaks of the guidance Allah granted to Moses and Aaron, which the commentators describe as the straight path with no crookedness. Most exegetes identify it with Islam, the religion of God that He sent through all His prophets. Al-Tabari, quoting Qatada, holds this view, and it is followed by al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir; al-Zamakhshari specifies that it is the path of the people of Islam. Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as the path of revealed law and prophethood leading to God. Al-Razi explains that the guidance meant showing them the way of truth by reason and revelation, supporting them with success and protection, the straight path being a figure for sound proofs. Al-Qurtubi defines it as the upright religion without crookedness, which is Islam. Al-Biqa'i sees a clear way leading to the goal, so firmly kept that it never deviates. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take it to include the details of the laws and the ramifications of the rulings. Ibn 'Ashur holds that it was the law of the Torah in Moses' time, later replaced by the Qur'an, while also allowing that it may mean the common foundations of faith such as monotheism. The verse belongs to a passage listing the favours given to Moses and Aaron: prophethood, deliverance, victory and the revealed Book. The commentators agree that the lasting good remembrance Allah left for them among later generations, and the peace upon them, are part of this honour. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi conclude that faith is the highest and most noble of virtues.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the list of favours bestowed on Moses and Aaron, and that it means God left them a lasting good name and praise among the generations that follow, so that they are greeted with peace and remembered with honour. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this "leaving" as the enduring good reputation itself, and al-Jalalayn, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani express the same meaning as a lasting praiseworthy remembrance. Most scholars link the verse to what precedes it: the prophethood, the rescue from oppression, the victory over Pharaoh, the clear Book and the straight path. The pronoun refers to both brothers. Al-Razi offers two readings of "the later generations": either the community of Muhammad, who say peace upon Moses and Aaron, or the good renown itself, in which case the words "Peace upon Moses and Aaron" are God's own speech. Ibn al-Qayyim, as reported by Ibn Sa'di, prefers to take the "leaving" as the greeting of peace, which persists among those who follow. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the greeting can only be said collectively by someone who joins their two names in the prayer. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur also see in the story of Moses and Aaron a lesson for the Prophet. The verse thus calls for remembering the righteous after their death, and for tying their goodness to their faith.

This verse recalls that God favoured Moses and Aaron with prophethood and delivered them and their people from the great distress, which most commentators, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya, take to mean the enslavement and oppression by Pharaoh, while al-Suddi and al-Zamakhshari understand it as the drowning of Pharaoh and his people. God then gave them victory so that they became the dominant ones, gave them the clear Book, which is the Torah, guided them to the straight path, and left them a good name among later generations, so that people say: peace be upon Moses and Aaron. The commentators explain that this is how God rewards those who do good, and that the reason is that they were believing servants. There is broad agreement that the straight path is the religion of Islam and that the Book is the Torah. Al-Farra' holds that the pronoun in the phrase 'and We gave them victory' refers to the two brothers alone, out of honour, while al-Tabari and most others include their people. Al-Razi observes that the verse combines the two kinds of blessing: bringing benefits and averting harms. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the greeting of peace is addressed to both brothers together, which he sees as unusual compared with the other verses about the prophets.

This passage of Surat as-Saffat recalls the favours God bestowed on Moses and Aaron: He honoured them with prophethood and mission, saved them and their people from the great distress, gave them victory, granted them the clear Book, which is the Torah, and guided them to the straight path. The verse concludes that God thus rewards the good-doers, because these two are among His believing servants. The commentators agree that the great distress was Pharaoh's enslavement and humiliation of the Children of Israel, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir also mention drowning, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports both views. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi identify the straight path with Islam, the religion of God that all the messengers brought; al-Zamakhshari adds that it is the path of those upon whom God has bestowed favour, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the law of the Torah was that path in its time before the Quran abrogated it. As for the lasting praise left among later generations, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn read it as a good reputation, whereas al-Razi attributes it to the community of Muhammad who greet them. Opinions also differ on the pronoun in 'We gave them victory': al-Farra', al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take it to refer to Moses, Aaron and their people, while others take it to refer only to the two prophets, out of honour. Ibn Sa'di stresses that God guided them with an upright law. The closing phrase, 'thus do We reward the good-doers', is explained by al-Jalalayn as the reward given to these two, and by Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi as tied to servitude and faith.

This verse recalls that God favoured Moses and Aaron with prophethood and rescued them and their people from Pharaoh. He gave them the clear Book, which the commentators agree is the Torah, and guided them to the straight path, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi identify with the religion of Islam, the faith of all the prophets. Al-Zamakhshari reads the straight path as the path of the people of Islam mentioned in al-Fatiha, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as the path of revealed law leading to God. God also left them a lasting good name among later generations, and the greeting of peace that follows is read by most as a blessing upon them. The verse ends by stating that God rewards the doers of good in this way, and that the two brothers were among His believing servants.

The commentators differ on the great distress from which they were delivered. Qatada, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take it to be Pharaoh's enslavement and persecution of the Israelites, whereas al-Sudd and others take it to be drowning. Al-Razi argues that the verse names two kinds of favour: bringing benefits and warding off harms. On the pronoun in 'We helped them', al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur prefer that it refers to Moses, Aaron and their people, while al-Farra' holds that it refers to the two brothers alone, as a mark of honour.

The closing phrase, that they were among God's believing servants, is explained by al-Tabari as meaning that they were sincere in their faith. Al-Razi observes that the mention of belief at the end points to faith as the highest of virtues, since it crowns the list of their merits.

This verse states that Ilyas was one of the messengers sent by God. The commentators say he was of the lineage of Aaron, brother of Moses, and was sent to the Israelites in the region of Baalbek in Syria, who worshipped an idol called Ba'l. He asked them whether they would not fear God, and how they could call upon Ba'l while abandoning God, the best of creators, their Lord and the Lord of their forefathers. The exegetes agree that Ba'l refers to an idol, but differ on the meaning of the word: Ikrima, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean 'lord' in the Yemeni dialect, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say it was the name of an idol, and Ibn Ishaq says it was a woman they worshipped. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi relate a long account of King Ajab and his wife Izabel and of Ilyas's trials, in which Ilyas is taken up to heaven according to some. Ibn Mas'ud read 'Idris' instead of Ilyas and identified the two, a view followed by Ikrima and Qatada, while most commentators regard Ilyas as a distinct Israelite prophet. As for the greeting 'Peace upon the family of Yasin', some read 'Al Yasin', which some interpret as the family of Muhammad, peace be upon him, but most take it to mean Ilyas and his believing followers. Regarding the phrase 'they will be brought forth to punishment', the commentators understand it as their being presented to the torment, except God's sincere servants.

These verses tell of the prophet Ilyas, one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, whom God sent to his people to call them to fear God and to stop worshipping the idol called Ba'l. The commentators explain that the verse rebukes them for not fearing God and His punishment. They differ on the meaning of the word "Ba'l": Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Qatada take it to mean "lord" in the dialect of Yemen, while al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say it was an idol they possessed, from which the city of Ba'albek takes its name, and Ibn Ishaq reports it was a woman they worshipped. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir regard these views as close in meaning, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that the first two are both valid, the idol being called lord by way of claim.

The commentators agree that Ilyas called his people to monotheism, that God kept a good name for him, that those who deny will be brought to punishment, and that only God's sincere servants will be spared. The readings differ on his name: most read "Ilyas" with a kasra hamza, Ibn 'Amir reads it with a linking hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud reads "Idris". Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and 'Ikrima held that this is Idris, but most exegetes, such as al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, state that he was a prophet of the Children of Israel from the line of Aaron.

As for the phrase "Al Yasin", some take it to mean Ilyas and his followers, while al-Kalbi and Ibn 'Abbas relate it to the family of Muhammad, a view Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur reject because the context refers to Ilyas. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report detailed accounts of the drought and of the restoration of a dead boy, which come from sources drawn from the People of the Book, and which the commentators do not regard as established.

This verse recounts the story of Elijah (Ilyas), a prophet sent to the Children of Israel, who rebuked his people for worshipping an idol called Ba'l and for abandoning the worship of God, the best of creators, urging them to fear God alone. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and the Jalalayn, hold that Ba'l is the name of an idol, and that the city of Ba'albek was named after it. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi report that it was made of gold, had four faces and four hundred attendants, and that the devil spoke from within it, though al-Razi finds part of this account problematic. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and Qatada explain that Ba'l means "lord" in the Yemeni dialect, relying on the anecdote of the man searching for his camel. Ibn Ishaq reports that it was a woman who was worshipped. On the prophet's name, Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada identify him with Idris, while the majority identify him as Ilyas son of Yasin, of Aaron's line. For the reading "Al Yasin", Ibn Abbas takes it as the family of Muhammad, whereas al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur take it as his followers. Al-Tabari considers the two readings of "Allah" (nominative and accusative) to be equivalent and both acceptable. Scholars differ on "ahsan al-khaliqin": some read it as the best of creators, others as the best of makers or measurers. Al-Razi rejects using the verse to argue that humans create their own acts, an argument made by the Mu'tazilites.

This verse belongs to the story of Elijah (Ilyas), who called his people to abandon the idol Baal and worship God alone. The commentators explain that God is the Lord of those addressed and of their earliest forefathers, so He alone deserves worship; hence the rebuke to those who call upon Baal and leave aside the best of creators. Most exegetes take the word Allah as an apposition or substitute for 'the best of creators', while the majority reading makes it nominative, as a new statement meaning 'He is God, your Lord'. Al-Tabari judges both readings close in meaning and both correct. The word Baal is explained by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and Qatada as meaning 'lord' in the dialect of Yemen, whereas al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say it was an idol they worshipped, from which the city of Baalbek took its name; Ibn Ishaq reports that it was a woman they worshipped. Zamakhshari holds that the meaning works under both views. Scholars also differ on Ilyas's identity: some, following Ibn Masud and Qatada, identify him with Idris, but most hold him to be a prophet of the Children of Israel from the line of Aaron. Many report that God sent him to an idolatrous people and that his life ended with his being taken up to heaven. The verses close with a greeting upon Ilyas and God's praise of him as one of His believing servants. Some read 'the family of Yasin' as Ilyas's kin or followers, others as the family of Muhammad. Ibn Kathir takes the exception to refer to the monotheists among his people, and as a discontinuous exception.

This part of the verse states that the people of Elijah denied him, so they will be brought forward to punishment on the Day of Resurrection, except for the sincere servants of God among them, who are saved. The commentators agree that the denial concerned what he called them to, namely the oneness of God and the abandonment of worship of the idol Ba'l. They differ on the meaning of being brought forward: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to mean being brought into God's punishment, while Abu al-Su'ud regards it as an unrestricted term whose context makes the negative sense clear. As for the exception, most scholars take it as a continuous exception, meaning that the sincere among his people did not deny him and were saved; Ibn Kathir considers it discontinuous, and al-Alusi allows both readings while preferring the first. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi present Elijah as a prophet of the Children of Israel, whereas Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and al-Dahhak identify him with Idris, an opinion most exegetes did not adopt. Regarding the phrase 'and We left for him a good name among the later generations', al-Tabari reads it as a lasting good mention, others as a greeting of peace upon him, and most combine both meanings.

This verse concerns the exception made in the story of Ilyas (Elijah) with his people: those who called him a liar will be brought forward for punishment, while God's sincere servants will be spared. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take this to mean that the believers among his people are the ones saved. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss whether the exception is connected to the pronoun of the deniers or stands separately, and both readings are reported. All agree that the "sincere" are the monotheists. The reading of "mukhlasin" varies between a kasra and a fatha on the lam: the first means those who devoted themselves sincerely to God, the second means those whom God chose. As for Ilyas's identity, Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada identify him with Idris, while the majority hold that he was Ilyas son of Yasin, from the line of Aaron. On the word "Ba'l", al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ikrima explain it as "lord" in the dialect of Yemen, whereas al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd understand it as an idol after which Baalbek was named. Several commentators relate lengthy accounts of the drought sent upon the people and of Ilyas being taken up on a chariot of fire, some of which are doubted or traced to Israelite narratives.

This part of the verse says that God left Elijah, peace be upon him, a lasting good name among the nations that came after him. The commentators tie the verse to his story with his people: he called them to fear God and to abandon the idol Ba'l, but they denied him, and God excepted His sincere servants from among them from the punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi agree that the phrase "We left for him among the later ones" means a lasting good praise. They differ on the grammar: most take the verb to mean "We let remain" with its object understood as a good praise, while Ibn al-Qayyim, as Ibn Kathir reports, holds that the object is the greeting of peace that follows. The greeting itself is read in two ways: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Ali Yasin" with "Al" joined to Yasin, while the majority read "Il Yasin." Al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari explain it as a variant of Ilyas or a plural meaning Ilyas and his followers; Ibn 'Abbas and others say it refers to the family of Muhammad, peace be upon him, while al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer that it means Ilyas and the believers who followed him. All agree that this lasting praise is a blessing from God and that reward for good is His established way.

The commentators explain that the verse conveys peace and greeting from God upon the 'family of Yasin', meaning Elias and those who believed with him, and that God thus rewards the good-doers as He rewarded Elias for his righteousness and faith. All agree that Elias was a prophet of the Children of Israel sent to a people who worshipped an idol called Ba'l, and that the verse closes his story with praise. They differ over the word 'Ilyasin': al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, followed by Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, took it as a plural meaning Elias and his followers, like 'al-Muhallabun', while Ibn Jinni held that the Arabs play freely with foreign names so that Yasin and Ilyas are one name, and others saw it as a dialectal variant of Ilyas, like Isma'il and Isma'in. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read 'Al Yasin' with the genitive; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir took it to mean Elias or his people, al-Kalbi took it to mean the family of Muhammad ﷺ, a view al-Wahidi and al-Biqa'i rejected as unsupported by the context. Ibn Mas'ud read 'Idrasin' and identified Elias with Idris, a view few adopted. On Ba'l, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said it meant 'lord' in the Yemeni dialect, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said it was an idol of Baalbek, and Ibn Ishaq said it was a woman they worshipped. The common thread is that Elias rebuked his people for worshipping other than God, who is their Lord and the Lord of their forefathers.

The commentators read this verse as the closing words of the story of Ilyas (Elijah): God rewards the doers of good, meaning those who worship and act well, in the same way He rewarded Ilyas, one of His believing servants. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Qurtubi note that this reward is the one promised to the believers, and that the phrase extends the judgment to every good-doer. Several authors stop at this meaning, while others link the verse to the greeting of peace upon Ilyas that precedes it.

The main disagreement concerns who Ilyas was. Ibn Mas'ud, Ikrima and Qatada, reported by Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Razi and Qurtubi, say he is Idris, whereas the majority, including Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that he was a prophet of the Children of Israel descended from Aaron. Abu Hayyan suggests that Ibn Mas'ud's reading was likely an explanation rather than a variant.

Scholars also differ on the name's form. Farra and Ibn Jinni treat Ilyasin as a dialectal form or a plural meaning Ilyas and his followers, while Tabari takes it simply as the name Ilyas, and Zamakhshari objects that a true plural would have taken the definite article. Tabari prefers the majority reading with a kasra and no alif after the lam, since the greeting of peace in the surah falls on the prophets themselves. The reading Al Yasin as the family of Muhammad, reported by Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, is judged unlikely by Wahidi and Baghawi because it has no earlier mention in the context.

Verse 37:132 describes Ilyas (Elijah) as "one of Our believing servants," closing the account of this prophet and his people in this passage. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that he was among the believers who worshipped God alone, obeyed Him and associated nothing with Him. The commentators agree that the verse praises him and makes his honour a reward for his good conduct, as Ibn Sa'di notes, and al-Qasimi links the reward to both ihsan and faith.

The main disagreement concerns who Ilyas is. Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ikrima, cited by al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, identify him with Idris (Enoch). Most exegetes, including al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya, hold that he was a prophet of the Children of Israel from the line of Aaron. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explain that the form "Ilyasin" may be a dialect variant of the name, or a plural meaning Ilyas and his followers; al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda prefer the reading of the majority, since "Al" is not normally used with a proper name alone.

The commentators report that his people worshipped the idol Ba'l, and that the surrounding passage contains his call to the oneness of God. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi specify that the believers meant are those who dedicated their worship to God. On the precise sense of ihsan and its relation to faith the opinions vary somewhat, and God knows best what He intended.

This verse states that Lot was among the messengers, and that God saved him and all his family from the punishment that fell on his people, except his wife, who remained among those left behind and perished with them. Commentators agree that the word "al-ghabirin" can mean either those left to endure the punishment or those who had already perished, and as-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Qatada, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud give both senses as close in meaning. Al-Tabari reports, through ad-Dahhak, that Lot's wife lagged behind and was turned into a stone, whereas Ibn Kathir only says she perished with her people. On the destruction, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe a rain of stones and various punishments, and Ibn Kathir adds that the place became a foul-smelling lake that travellers pass by day and night. Most exegetes read "You pass by their ruins" as addressed to the Quraysh, whose trade caravans went to Syria. Ibn 'Ashur notes that Lot brought no new law beyond forbidding the foul deed. Ibn 'Uthaymin points out that a believer may unknowingly be married to an unbeliever, and that one should watch over one's family.

In this verse God says that He saved Lot and all his family from the punishment He sent upon his people, who were destroyed. The commentators agree that the exception in the following verse refers to Lot's wife, who was an unbeliever and perished with her people. The meaning of "those who remained" (al-ghabirin) varies: as-Suddi takes it to mean "those who perished", Ibn Zayd "those left among the perished", Qatada "those who remain in the punishment", and Muqatil "those who passed on in the punishment". Ad-Dahhak reports that Lot's wife was turned into stone for lagging behind, but al-Farra' notes that this account does not belong to the exegesis that most scholars rely on.

Most commentators agree on the apparent sense: the salvation of Lot and the believers of his household, the ruin of the disbelievers, and the exclusion of Lot's wife. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the destruction came as a rain of stones, and that the place became a foul lake that travellers pass by day and night. Az-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse addresses the Quraysh, whose trade caravans to Syria passed by the towns of Lot's people, and calls them to take heed. Ibn 'Ashur adds that Lot was sent only to his own town, and that the prohibition of this sin had not been part of Abraham's law.

The verses that follow, about Elias, raise differences over the reading and identity of the name. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Mas'ud read "Idris", and Ibn Kathir and al-Farra' mention the readings "Al Yasin" with their various interpretations. This debate, however, does not affect the main meaning of Lot's deliverance.

This verse recalls that Lot, peace be upon him, was among the messengers, and that God saved him and all his family from the punishment that destroyed his people, except his wife, who remained among those who were destroyed. The commentators agree on the general meaning, but differ on the word al-ghabirin. Al-Sudi, Ibn Zayd, Qatada and Muqatil understood it as those who perished or those left behind in punishment, while al-Mawardi lists four possible meanings without preferring one. Al-Tabari reports, through al-Dahhak, that the woman lagged behind and was turned into stone. Ibn Atiyya states that she was an unbeliever, whether she hid her disbelief or displayed it, and that marriage to idolaters was then permitted. Abu Hayyan explains that her disbelief excluded her from the saved group, and al-Biqa'i sees her disbelief as severing the close tie.

The commentators also agree on the rest of the passage, in which God rained stones upon that people, and on the fact that the people of Mecca passed by their ruins morning and night on their trading journeys to the Levant. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari draw from this a call to reflect and take a lesson. Ibn Ashur notes that Lot was a messenger without a law of his own, sent to forbid the immorality of those among whom he lived. Ibn Sa'di and al-Alusi add that the mention of the time of deliverance shows that Lot was then carrying out his mission.

This verse states that after Lot and his believing family were saved, with the exception of his wife who stayed with the disbelievers and perished with them, God destroyed the rest, meaning the remainder of his people who had rejected him. Commentators gloss the verb as bringing ruin or destruction. Al-Tabari describes it as stones hurled down upon them from above, while Ibn Kathir reports that God turned their land into a foul, stinking lake that travellers pass by day and night. Al-Qasimi mentions the overturning of the town so that its upper part became its lower part, along with a rain of hardened clay stones. Al-Jalalayn and Ibn Sa'di give a general description of annihilation, which Ibn Sa'di links to this overturning. On the meaning of "al-ghabirin", applied to Lot's wife, opinions differ: al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it to mean those who perished, Qatada those who remain in punishment, and Muqatil those who have passed away. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani note that the rescue of Lot and the destruction of his people show the truth of his mission. All commentators connect the closing lines to the Meccans, who pass the ruins on their trading journeys to Syria, so that they may take warning and reflect.

In this verse God addresses the people of Makkah, the Quraysh, reminding them that on their trading journeys to Syria they pass by the dwellings of Lot's people, whom God destroyed with punishment, both in the morning and at night. The commentators explain that the passing is over their traces and dwellings, and that it happens at both times of day, since travel is done early in the morning and by night. Some, however, take "in the morning" to mean the whole day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur agree that the verse is an admonition and a rebuke: "Will you not then reason?", that is, will you not learn from what befell those who denied their messengers, so that you abandon polytheism and denial. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that the address is directed squarely at the Quraysh, who could see these ruins with their own eyes. Ibn Kathir adds that the place became a foul-smelling lake that travelers cross day and night. The commentators stress that true reason is what guides its owner to good and away from evil, and that cleverness alone is not enough. Ibn Ashur notes that the informative form is used here to awaken and to prompt reflection. Other details, such as the timing of the passage or the extent of the ruins, are reported without the scholars settling between them.

In this verse God addresses the Quraysh of Mecca and reminds them that they pass by the dwellings and remains of Lot's people, in the morning and at night, on their trading journeys to Syria. He then rebukes them with the question: will you not use your reason? That is, will you not take a lesson from what befell those places and fear that the same fate may strike you? The commentators agree that the address is to Quraysh, and that the verse follows the story of Lot to serve as a warning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe the remains as a foul, stinking lake that now occupies the site of the destroyed towns, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi speak simply of passing by their dwellings. Ibn 'Ashur identifies the place as the shore of the Dead Sea, whose ruins still lie beneath the water. On the timing of the passage, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani understand the morning and the night as the whole of day and night, whereas al-Alusi prefers the evening or the start of the night, and others take it as morning and evening. Several scholars, including al-Biqa'i and al-Razi, stress that seeing the traces directly gives a stronger conviction than hearing about them, and that true reason is what guides a person away from evil. They also note that rejecting the messenger was the cause of the destruction. No separate legal ruling derived from this verse is reported in these commentaries.

This verse affirms that Yunus, son of Matta, was among the messengers. The sentence is emphasised with inna and the lam of confirmation, because many people deny prophetic mission. The commentators explain that Yunus, a prophet of the Children of Israel, was sent to his people in Nineveh. When they refused to believe and the punishment he had announced did not arrive, he left them in anger and boarded a crowded ship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the word ibaq, the flight of a runaway slave, as an image of his leaving without God's permission, while al-Razi and others argue that a prophet does not disobey and that this was an unordered departure. The commentators agree that lots were cast among the passengers, that the lot fell on Yunus, and that a great fish swallowed him. They acknowledge that his departure was blameworthy, but differ on how long he stayed in the fish's belly: a moment, three days, seven days or forty days. All report that his rescue came through his earlier glorification and prayer, and that the fish cast him ashore weakened, after which God made a gourd plant grow over him. He was then sent to a hundred thousand people or more, who believed and were granted a time of enjoyment. Regarding the particle aw, some read it as meaning bal (rather), others as a precision, and the estimates of the excess range from twenty thousand to seventy thousand. The shared lesson is that devotion in ease sustains one in hardship, and that the story consoles the Prophet over his people's disbelief.

The commentators explain that Jonah, after being sent to his people, left them in anger when the punishment he had announced did not fall upon them. He boarded a ship loaded with passengers and cargo. The vessel became stuck in the open sea, and the crew cast lots to determine who should be thrown overboard to lighten it; the lot fell on Jonah, who was then swallowed by the fish while blameworthy. All agree that his flight, called ibaq, was a departure from his people without God's permission, a word originally used for a runaway slave and borrowed here by analogy. On the meaning of mudhdahin, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say those defeated by the lot, Sa'id ibn Jubayr says those overcome, and al-Suddi says those whose argument is refuted. As for the glorification that saved him, Ibn Abbas, Muqatil and Ibn Jubayr take it to be prayer or frequent remembrance of God, al-Hasan takes it to be his words 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers', and Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to be good deeds performed in ease. Most say that otherwise the fish's belly would have become his grave. The length of his stay in the fish is reported differently: an hour, three days, seven days, forty days, with no decisive proof for any of them. The tree of yaqtin is identified by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas as the gourd, while others say any plant without a stalk. On the second mission, Ibn Abbas places it after his release from the fish, Mujahid before he was swallowed, and others link it to a different people. The 'or' in 'a hundred thousand or more' is read as 'rather', as 'and', or as a estimate from the observer's view, and the figures given for the excess range from twenty thousand to seventy thousand.

This verse recounts the story of Yunus, who, though one of the messengers, fled in anger from his people towards a ship laden with passengers. When the vessel was tossed by the sea, the crew cast lots to choose one to be thrown overboard, and the lot fell on him, so he was among those defeated by the drawing. A fish then swallowed him while he was blameworthy, meaning he had done something deserving of blame. The commentators agree that al-musahama means casting lots and that al-mudhdahin means those defeated by the lot, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Mujahid explain, though al-Suddi also takes it to mean an argument being refuted, while Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya describe it as slipping from a position of victory. Regarding mulim, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd say it means guilty, Qatada says one who blames himself, and al-Kalbi says one who is blamed. They agree that his glorification of God, in the fish's belly or earlier in ease, was what saved him. They differ on how long he stayed inside: Dahhak says twenty days, Ata seven days, and al-Sha'bi part of a single day. He was then cast out onto bare ground, weakened, and God made a gourd plant grow over him, before he was sent to a hundred thousand people or more, who believed and were granted enjoyment for a time. Ibn Abbas reads the particle aw as meaning "rather," while others take it as a confirmation of the figure.

According to the commentaries, Yunus (Jonah), distressed by his people and having left them without God's leave, boarded a ship overloaded with passengers. It stopped in mid-sea, and the crew cast lots to choose whom to throw overboard to lighten it; the lot fell on him, he was cast into the water, and the fish swallowed him while he was 'mulim', that is, having done something deserving blame. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree on the basic account: he was swallowed and kept safe in the fish's belly, and his departure was without divine command, though they differ on whether the blame came from others or from himself. They also agree that his rescue was owed to his earlier glorification of God. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take this to mean prayer in times of ease; al-Hasan takes it to mean prayer inside the fish; Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies it with his words 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers'. The length of his stay in the fish is disputed, with reports of three, seven, twenty or forty days, and no decisive preference is given. Scholars also differ on whether his mission came before or after his swallowing: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid favour before, others after. On the phrase 'or they were more', Ibn 'Abbas reads it as 'rather they were more', while others read it as a form of approximation, and the figures given for the excess vary. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi use the episode to discuss casting lots, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that it does not by itself establish that practice as lawful in our law beyond the cases the Prophet recognised.

This verse in Surah al-Saffat states that had Jonah not been among those who glorify God, he would have remained inside the fish until the Day of Resurrection, and it was his earlier devotion that saved him. The commentators agree that tasbih here means glorifying God in general, through prayer and worship. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-'Aliya and Qatada understand it as prayer, while Wahb ibn Munabbih understands it as worship. Al-Hasan holds that it refers to a prayer Jonah performed inside the fish, a view that Qatada and 'Imran al-Qattan reject. Ibn Jubayr reads it as the formula 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was indeed among the wrongdoers', which al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya also adopt. Al-Razi prefers a glorification of the tongue matching the heart, and al-Qurtubi considers this the most likely meaning, performed inside the fish. The commentators differ on how long he stayed: part of a day, three days, seven days, twenty days or forty days, and none decides the matter with a conclusive proof. As for the plant that shaded him, most identify the yaqtin as the gourd, following Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, while others describe it as any creeping plant without a stem, such as the melon or colocynth, or any plant that dies within the same year. Thus the commentators agree on the meaning of tasbih and Jonah's rescue, but differ on the length of his ordeal and the exact nature of the plant.

This verse says that Jonah, swallowed by the fish for fleeing without his Lord's leave, would have remained in its belly until the Resurrection had he not been among those who glorify God. The commentators generally agree on the lesson: good deeds and remembrance of God in ease bring rescue in hardship. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir report that most understood the glorification as prayer, as Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, while al-Hasan held that he had no prayer in the fish but that his words were the invocation 'there is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers', a view Sa'id ibn Jubayr also gave. They differ on how long he stayed inside: three days according to Qatada and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, seven according to Ata', forty according to al-Sudi and al-Kalbi, and a few hours according to others. Cast onto bare ground, he was weak like a newborn, and God caused a gourd plant (yaqtin) to grow over him; most identify it with the squash, though others describe any plant spreading along the ground. Regarding the people he was sent to, a hundred thousand or more, Ibn Abbas spoke of thirty thousand more, others gave different figures, and the commentators debate whether 'aw' means 'rather' or merely confirms the number. Those people believed when they saw the punishment, and God let them enjoy life until their appointed term.

This passage recounts the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, as the commentators relate it. Once cast out by the fish, he was left on open ground with no tree or shade, weak and worn, like a newborn child. The exegetes agree that his deliverance was a gift from God, but they differ on what saved him. Al-Hasan and others hold that it was his words, 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was indeed among the wrongdoers', while Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya understand it as the prayer and remembrance he had practised abundantly in times of ease; al-Tabari favours this latter view. As for how long he stayed in the fish, the reports vary between a moment, three days, seven days and forty days, and no single view is settled.

The tree that God caused to grow over him is, for most commentators such as Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Mas'ud, the gourd plant; the word yaqtin is taken to mean any plant that spreads along the ground without a stem, and some include any plant that dies within the year. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also relate the report that a wild doe came to nurse him, but they transmit it without deciding its authenticity.

The commentators also differ on the sending to a hundred thousand or more. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada take it to be a mission after his release from the fish, whereas Mujahid and al-Hasan place it before he was swallowed. On the particle 'aw', al-Farra' and Muqatil read it as 'indeed, more', while al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj take it as the estimate of the observer. The size of the excess varies among reports between twenty, thirty and seventy thousand, and none is preferred.

This verse says that after the fish cast Yunus onto bare ground, God made a gourd-plant (yaqtin) grow over him to shade and shelter him. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, identify it as the gourd or squash plant, noting its broad leaves, its cool shade, and the fact that flies avoid it; they also recall that the Prophet ﷺ loved this fruit and picked it from the edge of the dish. Others, such as al-Mubarrad, define yaqtin more generally as any low-growing plant without a stem, such as the melon, cucumber or colocynth, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan suggest God may have made it grow with a stem, contrary to custom. Al-Zamakhshari describes it as a canopy spread over him like a tent. Several accounts say a wild doe came to feed him with her milk until he regained strength, and al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur describe his gradual recovery. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi relate that he wept when the plant withered and was rebuked for grieving over a tree while not grieving over the hundred thousand people, but Ibn 'Uthaymin doubts the doe story as it lacks authentic transmission and treats such details as unverified Israelite material. Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress God's care for Yunus in this moment.

This verse states that God sent Yunus to a hundred thousand people or more, and that they believed and were allowed to enjoy life until their appointed term. The commentators agree that these are the people to whom Yunus was sent, but they differ on when this mission took place. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, followed by Ibn Kathir, place it after Yunus came out of the fish's belly, though Ibn Kathir allows that the first mission may simply have been repeated. Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that it happened before the fish swallowed him, and Ibn al-Jawzi considers this the sounder view, the particle wa then indicating the joining of events rather than their sequence. As for the word 'aw' in 'aw yazidun', Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Farra' and Muqatil take it to mean 'bal', that is 'rather, even more', while al-Zajjaj, al-Mubarrad and many Basran grammarians read it as an estimate made by the observer, who would say 'they are a hundred thousand or more', the point being to stress their great number. The commentators differ on the size of the excess: twenty thousand according to a report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, thirty thousand according to Ibn 'Abbas, seventy thousand according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Finally, according to Qatada and al-Suddi, the favour granted lies in their being allowed to live until the end of their lives, having believed when they saw the punishment approaching, which God then lifted.

This verse states that Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to his people, the people of Nineveh near Mosul, numbering a hundred thousand or more, and that they believed. God then allowed them to enjoy life until the end of their appointed terms. The commentators agree that this faith came after they saw the signs of the punishment, and that God lifted it because they repented. As for the phrase 'for a time', most explain it as the end of their lifespans, and al-Tabari reports from Qatada and al-Suddi that it means death. They differ on when this mission took place. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and most scholars, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, place it after the fish had cast him onto the shore, whereas Mujahid, al-Hasan and others hold that it came before he was swallowed, the particle 'and' (waw) then indicating only the joining of events rather than their order. On the word 'or' in 'a hundred thousand or more', Ibn Abbas and al-Farra' take it to mean 'rather', while others read it as vagueness or as a estimate from the observer's viewpoint. The exact size of the excess also varies in the reports: a hadith transmitted through Ubayy ibn Ka'b speaks of twenty thousand, Ibn Abbas mentions thirty thousand, Sa'id ibn Jubayr seventy thousand, and others suggest some thirty or forty thousand. Al-Zamakhshari and others note, however, that the purpose is to convey great numbers rather than to fix a precise figure.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to question the Quraysh with rebuke and reproach: how can you attribute daughters to your Lord while reserving sons for yourselves? The commentators agree that this refers to the claim of some Arab tribes, such as Juhayna, Banu Salama, Khuza'a and Banu Malih, that the angels are God's daughters. The question is mocking and condemnatory. Ibn Kathir explains that the Arabs disliked having daughters, so this division is unjust. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw three corruptions from the claim: sonship implies corporeality, it places themselves above God, and it demeans the angels by making them female. As for the question whether God created the angels as females while they were witnesses, most commentators take it as a refutation: no one witnessed their creation, so their claim is a lie. Opinions differ on the word jinna in the phrase that they made a kinship between Him and the jinn. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Qurtubi take it to mean the angels, while al-Hasan, Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean the jinn, and Ibn Abbas also reports the view that God and Iblis were brothers. Ibn Kathir reads the statement that the jinn know as meaning that they know these people will be brought to punishment. Ibn Ashur holds that the pronoun in the command to question them refers to someone understood from the context.

This verse rebukes the polytheists who claimed that the angels are daughters of God. The question is one of reproach: did they witness the creation of the angels so as to say they are female? The implied answer is no, so their claim is baseless falsehood. The commentators agree that this saying is a lie and that God is exalted above having offspring. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that those who said this were groups from Quraysh, Khuza'a, Juhayna and Banu Mudlij, while al-Sam'ani notes that only some of Quraysh held it. As for the claim of kinship between God and the jinn, al-Mawardi lists several views: some take it as associating Satan with God's worship, others as an alliance claimed by the Jews, and others as the belief of the zindiqs that God and Iblis are brothers. Mujahid explains that the angels could be called jinn because they are hidden, but most exegetes, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, understand the word to refer to the jinn themselves. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy describe the verse as a sharp refutation, and al-Razi gives rational arguments: divine perfection excludes choosing the lesser, and every claim needs proof. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Kathir note that the particle (am) here is disjunctive, meaning rather. Al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani mention various readings of the opening of (istafa), but the interrogative reading remains the most widespread.

This passage shows God instructing His Prophet to question the Meccan pagans with rebuke: how can they assign daughters to God, which they themselves dislike, while keeping sons for themselves? God then states that the angels were not witnesses to their creation, so they cannot claim them to be female, and He calls their claim that the angels are God's daughters a plain lie: they lie in saying God has a son. The commentators agree that this belief is false and that the questions in these verses are rhetorical reproach rather than genuine inquiry, the aim being to declare God free of offspring and spouse. Ibn Kathir and others note that those who said this were Arab polytheists, and some stress the injustice of their division, which gives God the lesser share and keeps the better for themselves. The main point of disagreement concerns the reading of 'asṭafā': most read it with an interrogative hamza, expressing denial, while Nafi' in one transmission, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Hamza read it without interrogation, as a report of the unbelievers' words; al-Zamakhshari judges this reading weak, whereas Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan consider it possible while holding that the reproach surrounds the sentence. Commentators also differ on the meaning of 'al-Jinna': according to Mujahid and most exegetes it means the angels, so called because they are hidden, while others take it to mean the jinn, or, following Qatada, the Jews who claimed God had married into the jinn. As for the exception 'the sincere servants of God', Ibn Kathir considers it disjunctive, while others treat it as continuous. Taken together, the passage refutes the belief in divine descent through arguments drawn from the senses, from testimony and from reason.

This verse concerns the claim of the polytheists that God has begotten a child, and describes it as a manifest lie on their part. The commentators explain that by their falsehood they say that God has a son, and that in saying so they are liars. Qatada explains that the word ifk means falsehood. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir clarify that their words 'God has begotten' mean they made the angels God's daughters, which is among the gravest of lies. Ibn Juzayy regards the verse as a parenthetical remark placed among the other verses of the questioning, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi explain that it aims to refute the very basis of their doctrine, which rests on nothing but pure falsehood.

The commentators agree that the verse reproaches them for asserting things without knowledge or proof. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the three sources of knowledge, namely the senses, reliable testimony and reasoning, are all absent from this claim, and that the double emphasis with 'inna' and the lam signals the strength of the rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari lists three kinds of disbelief contained in this statement: anthropomorphism, preferring themselves over their Lord, and belittling the honoured angels.

As for the recitation, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi report that some readers joined the word 'istafa' to what precedes it, making it a statement rather than a question, while the majority reading keeps it as an interrogation of reproach. Al-Zamakhshari judges this second reading weak, because the negation surrounds the sentence on both sides, though others consider it acceptable.

In this verse God rebukes those who claimed that the angels are His daughters. He asks them, in a tone of astonishment, how He could choose for Himself daughters, whom they regarded as inferior, while keeping the sons they considered superior. Most commentators read the interrogative 'a-stafā' as a rebuke and a denial, the hamza being an interrogative particle after which the connecting alif was dropped. Some read 'istafā' as a declarative statement, and al-Zamakhshari and others take it as a quotation of their own words; most judge this reading weak, though Ibn 'Atiyya reports it without deciding. The commentators agree that the verses refute the claim by three means: the pagans did not witness the creation of the angels, they have no scripture to support it, and reason cannot hold that the most excellent would choose the lowest. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that Quraysh and some Arab tribes held this view. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi mention a different account, that God married women of the jinn, from whom the angels were born. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record several explanations of 'al-Jinna' and 'nasab', ranging from marriage ties to the belief of some that God and Iblis were brothers. All agree that the exception in 'except the sincere servants of God' is disjunctive: those sincere servants are spared from such claims.

This part of the verse rebukes the pagans for their claim that the angels are God's daughters. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir onward, read it as a reproach: how can you judge in this way? They assign to God the daughters, which they dislike for themselves, and keep the sons for themselves. Al-Tabari explains that this is a bad judgment, and Ibn Kathir recalls the verse describing a man's face darkening at news of a daughter. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the interrogation expresses reproach and astonishment and follows the previous question directly.

The commentators agree that the verse belongs to a continuous argument. God demands proof, and their lack of proof condemns them. Al-Razi argues that three sources of knowledge are missing: direct observation, reliable report, and rational reasoning. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi stress the contradiction of giving the lesser to the Creator and the better to themselves.

The reading of the word for 'chose' differs. Most read it with an interrogative hamza, while Abu Ja'far, Nafi' in one transmission, and Hamza read it without, as a statement reporting the pagans' words. Al-Zamakhshari judges this reading weak, because the negation surrounds the sentence on both sides. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse links directly to the preceding question.

God rebukes the Quraysh, who claimed that the angels are God's daughters, for assigning daughters to Him while they themselves would not accept daughters for themselves. The phrase "Will you not then remember?" invites them to reflect on what they say so that they recognize the error and stop. Al-Tabari reads it as a call to reflection and awareness, and Ibn Kathir sees in it a rejection of the unjust division they attributed to God. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a reproach for plain ignorance, the tone expressing astonishment and mockery. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy stress that a perfect being does not choose the lesser, and that reason alone refutes the claim, while Ibn Sa'di notes that an assertion without proof cannot be accepted. The commentators agree that God cannot have offspring. On recitation, Hamza, Hafs and al-Kisa'i read "tadhakkarun" with a single taa and a lighter form, while the common reading is "tadhdhakkarun" with assimilation. The commentaries mention no legal ruling on this point. The passage continues with a challenge: let them bring a Book that supports their claim, otherwise their assertions are false.

God rebukes the polytheists who claimed that the angels are daughters of God, asking them in a tone of reproach whether they have a clear authority for their claim. The commentators agree that the verse is a condemnation of their assertion and a demand for proof. Qatada and al-Suddi understood the word sultan as an excuse or proof, while Ibn Qutayba and al-Kalbi took it to mean a clear argument or a manifest book. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di hold that such proof can only come from a book sent down from heaven or from a messenger, since the matter is unseen and cannot be known by the senses or by reason alone. Ibn al-Qayyim, quoting Ibn Abbas, notes that every sultan in the Quran means a proof, because the one who holds the proof has power over his opponent. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi stress that their claim rests on no witness and no reliable report. Al-Razi argues that knowledge of it is unavailable through the senses, through trustworthy report, or through reasoning. The commentators also discuss the kinship (nasab) that the polytheists supposedly drew between God and the jinn. Al-Hasan understood it as associating Satan with God in worship, while Qatada and others took it to mean that God had married among the jinn. Some held that al-jinna refers to the angels because they are hidden from sight, while most identify them as the jinn. Al-Zamakhshari sees the passage as refuting three errors: anthropomorphism, preferring oneself to the Lord, and belittling those whom God honours. The point on which the views converge is that the verse is a severe rejection of their claim and a challenge to produce a proof they cannot provide.

This passage of Surat As-Saffat rebukes the Quraysh and others who claimed that the angels are God's daughters, while they preferred sons for themselves and disliked daughters. The commentators explain that the question in the verse is a reproach and a rebuke, that none of them witnessed the creation of the angels so as to judge them female, and that the claim is a lie. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the phrase 'Bring your book, if you are truthful' as a demand for a clear proof, namely a scripture sent down from heaven that supports their claim. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan stress the strong indignation and the mockery of the reasoning, which they see as exposing the folly of the Quraysh. As for the word 'jinna' in 'they have set up a kinship between Him and the jinn', Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean the angels, who are so called because they are hidden from sight, while al-Kalbi and al-Hasan point to the jinn or to the devils. Ibn Kathir holds that those who make this claim will be brought to punishment, and al-Razi notes that the exception in 'except the sincere servants of God' may be taken as disconnected. Some report that Abu Bakr asked about the mothers of the angels and was told they were the chiefs' daughters among the jinn, a report cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. All agree that God is exalted above having offspring and above every imperfection, and that His sincere servants never attribute such things to Him.

This verse speaks of the claim of the polytheists that there was a kinship (nasab) between God and "the Jinnah". The commentators differ on who is meant by the term. Most, including Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand it as the angels, named so because they are hidden from sight, and the kinship as their claim that the angels are God's daughters. Al-Tabari and Mujahid report that Abu Bakr asked them who the mothers were, and they answered: the daughters of the chiefs of the jinn. Al-Hasan reads the kinship as associating the devils with God in worship. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and others report that some said God and Iblis were brothers, or that God married among the jinn and the angels were born of that union; Qatada attributes this to the Jews, Mujahid and al-Suddi to the tribes of Kinana and Khuza'a. Al-Razi considers the dualist idea of a good god and an evil god the closest view, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that the Jinnah are the jinn themselves and that the kinship is a marital alliance, rejecting the angel interpretation. On "they will be brought forth", Mujahid takes it to mean judgment, whereas Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others take it to mean punishment in the Fire; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi prefer this because the same verb elsewhere in the surah refers to punishment. All agree that the sentence glorifies God above these claims and that His sincere servants are free of them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat the exception as disconnected, a view not shared by all.

In this verse God declares His immunity from what the idolaters attribute to Him, namely offspring or kinship with the jinn. The commentators agree that the verse clears God of these accusations. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, that some Quraysh claimed the angels were God's daughters, whose mothers were from the leading jinn; another report from Ibn 'Abbas says that God and Iblis were brothers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the phrase "the jinn knew that they would be brought forward" means that those who speak this way will be brought to punishment, and they judge this reading more correct than the one that refers it to the Day of Reckoning, which Mujahid preferred. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of "jinna", relating it either to the angels, who are hidden from sight, or to the jinn. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the exception "except the sincere servants of God" as disjunctive, meaning that sincere believers are safe and do not speak this way. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that the exception may also be read as connected, and that the word "mukhlasin" can mean those who are sincere in their worship or those whom God has made sincere. Ibn Sa'di observes that kinship does not fit with humble servitude. The commentators agree that the verse affirms that God has no offspring or consort and resembles no creature.

This clause states that God is exempt from the false description the polytheists attribute to Him, and that the "sincere servants of God" are excluded from it. The commentators agree on the context: the preceding verses report the claim that the angels are God's daughters and that there is a kinship between Him and the jinn. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada several explanations of this kinship: some say God and Iblis are brothers, others that God married among the jinn and the angels issued from that union, and others that it means associating Satan with the worship of God.

On the meaning of "al-jinna", most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, take it to be the angels, so called because they are hidden from sight. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer the demons. Al-Razi lists several views, including the idea that the kinship described recalls Zoroastrian or Manichaean dualism.

As for the exception, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy treat it as disconnected: the sincere servants are saved, or they are innocent of such an attribution. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan offer other readings, including one that links the exception to the damned. Ibn 'Ashur considers it disconnected and identifies the sincere servants as the angels themselves. Several scholars, including al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di, add that sincerity consists in describing God only by what befits Him.

This verse, in the context of rebutting those who attributed daughters to God and claimed a kinship between Him and the jinn, declares that neither the idols nor their worshippers can lead anyone astray, except one whom God has already decreed, in His knowledge, to be among the people of Hell. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak read it this way, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi follow the same sense. Al-Qurtubi reports that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz used it against the Qadariyya to affirm divine decree. The commentators differ on what the pronoun in 'upon it' refers to: most link it to the seduction of people, while al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Alusi, takes it to refer to God, meaning that they cannot corrupt His servants against Him. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy discuss whether the 'wa' before 'what you worship' means 'and' or 'together with', and whether 'ma' is relative or verbal. On al-Hasan's reading 'sali al-Jahim' with a damma, al-Tabari cites a poet and al-Nahhas calls it a solecism, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya offer grammatical explanations. The passage then moves to the angels, who say that each of them has a known station with God, that they stand in rows and glorify Him, as narrated through Ibn Mas'ud and Aisha. The general meaning on which all agree is a refutation of idolatry through the affirmation of God's absolute power.

The commentators explain that God addresses the polytheists, telling them that neither they nor what they worship can lead anyone astray, except one whom God has already decreed in His knowledge to be of the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi understand this as meaning that misguidance falls under the divine decree and that the idols cannot seduce anyone without God's permission. Al-Zamakhshari takes the pronoun in 'alayhi' to refer to God, meaning you cannot corrupt His servants against Him, while most exegetes refer it to the deities or to the worship. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that the waw in 'wa ma ta'budun' may be a conjunction or mean 'together with', and that the address may include the unseen powers that misled people. For the reading 'sālū al-jahīm' with a damma, the grammarians offer several explanations; al-Nahhas considers it a grammatical error, while others read it as following the sense of 'man'. The commentators then cite the words of the angels: each has a known station before God, they stand in rows and glorify Him, and some cite hadiths from Aisha and Ibn Mas'ud about the heavens filled with prostrating and standing angels. Finally, regarding 'had we a reminder from the ancients', they explain that the Quraysh had wished, before prophethood, to receive a Book so they would become sincere worshippers; when the Quran came they rejected it, and God warns that they will soon know the consequences of their disbelief.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the idolaters and those they worship cannot lead anyone astray except the one whom God has already decreed, in His foreknowledge, to be of the people of the Blazing Fire. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that misguidance happens only by God's decree and prior knowledge, so that 'one who is destined for the Blaze' means one whose wretchedness has been written. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to mean someone who is himself astray like them and deserves the Fire by his bad deeds. Al-Zamakhshari also notes that the pronoun 'upon him' may refer to God, meaning they cannot turn His servants against Him, whereas most commentators take it to refer to what is worshipped. The exegetes agree that 'fatinin' means 'leading astray'; al-Farra' notes that the people of the Hijaz say fatanahu and the people of Najd say aftanahu.

The words 'there is none of us but has a known station' are spoken by the angels. Most commentators read this as a fixed station in the heavens from which each angel worships God; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a hadith from 'A'isha that there is no space the width of a foot in the heavens without an angel standing or prostrating, and Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say the same. Al-Mawardi reports another view, that this station is the place of standing before God on the Day of Resurrection. 'Those who stand in ranks' and 'those who glorify' refer to the angels who form rows and proclaim God's glory; Qatada takes the latter to mean those who pray. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that Umar urged worshippers to straighten their rows after the example of the angels.

The reading of al-Hasan with a damma on the lam (sâlû) is treated by most as a plural construed according to the sense of 'man'; al-Nahhas and many exegetes call it a grammatical error, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari offer grammatical justifications. Briefer commentators such as al-Mahalli and the Jalalayn confine themselves to the meaning that only those whom God's knowledge has so decreed will be led astray.

The commentators explain that this verse records the words of the angels: each of them has a known station, which he does not exceed and from which he does not move, namely the place of worship and of submission to God's command. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the reference to be to the angels, and understand this worship as humble submission to God's greatness. Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say that every angel has a known place in the heavens where he worships God, and Ibn 'Abbas says there is not a span of the heavens without an angel praying or glorifying God. Many also cite the hadith of Abu Dhar about the heaven that creaks, with no space of four fingers without an angel prostrating.

The exegetes agree that this verse, together with the next, refutes the polytheists who claimed the angels were God's daughters. The angels are servants charged with worship, who stand in ranks in obedience and glorify God, so they cannot be partners of God. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Biqa'i and al-Nasafi understand the ones who stand in ranks as those who line up for prayer or in their station of worship, while Zamakhshari holds that they stand around the Throne or hold their wings in the air, awaiting the command.

Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur report that some traditions connect the verse to the rows of believers in prayer, and that Umar would order the rows straightened in imitation of the angels. Al-Qurtubi and others mention an opinion that the station belongs to each believer or messenger on the Day of Resurrection, but most keep the view that these are the angels' words. Grammarians also differed over the implied wording: the Basrans supply 'there is none of us who is not', and the Kufans 'none of us except one who has a station'.

In this verse, God relays the words of the angels: they stand in ranks in their places of worship and submission, and they glorify and exalt God. The commentators explain these ranks in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early exegetes understand them as the angels standing in rows in heaven or around the Throne, or as their lining up in prayer, with feet or wings spread. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi connect this with the believers' rows in prayer, and the hadith of Jabir ibn Samura about the angels' rows is cited in this sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse to call worshippers to straighten their rows. Several also cite traditions that no span of heaven is empty of an angel standing or prostrating, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir mention. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya note that 'tasbih' may mean prayer or the saying of glory to God, and that the angels thereby deny being divine beings, as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir argue. Al-Razi finds in these words three kinds of angelic qualities, in service and in knowledge of God. Some commentators, such as al-Mawardi, attribute the verse to the Prophet's words or to the believers, while Ibn Juzayy reads it as a description of the angels. The following verses recount the claim of the Quraysh that had they received a reminder from the ancients they would have been sincere servants of God; yet they rejected the Qur'an, and God warns that they will soon know.
