This verse records the words of the angels: they are servants of God, each with a known station in obedience from which he does not step aside, standing in ranks to worship Him, and glorifying God above whatever is unfitting for Him. Commentators explain the 'those who stand in ranks' as angels arrayed in the heavens around the Throne or in prayer, al-Kalbi comparing their rows to human rows on earth, while others take it as lined-up feet in prayer. For 'those who glorify', Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand those who pray or who declare God free of imperfection, and al-Nasafi includes prayer; most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, take the speakers to be the angels, and the overall sense is a rebuttal of those who claimed the angels are God's daughters. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur note that the words could also be the Prophet's and the believers', though the first reading is the better known. Several commentators report that before his mission the Quraysh wished for a Book like those given to earlier peoples so they would become sincere worshippers; when the Quran came they rejected it, and 'they will come to know' is read as a warning. Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take 'al-Jinna' to mean the angels in this context, while Abu Hayyan judges the apparent sense to point to the devils. Scholars also discuss, in connection with the verses before it, how far misguidance is attributed to God's decree rather than to human choice.

In this verse God quotes the angels, who say that they stand in ranks to worship Him and glorify Him, and then He reports what the idolaters of Mecca used to say before the Prophet's mission: if a reminder from the earlier peoples had come to us, we would have been sincere servants of God. The commentators agree that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh and the other Arabs, and that the particle «in» is the lightened form of «inna», with the «la» marking the distinction. Most of them take the passage as ending in reproach: the reminder, which is the greatest of reminders, has come, and they rejected it, so God warns that they will soon know the consequence of their disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the ones who stand in ranks as the angels arrayed in the heavens and the glorifiers as those who pray and declare God free of all defect, and Ibn Kathir cites several hadiths on this point. Omar ibn al-Khattab, as transmitted by Abu Nadra, told the believers to straighten their rows after the manner of the angels, an idea Ibn al-Jawzi also records. As for the phrase about each of us having a known station, Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean that each angel has a fixed place in the sky, while Qatada reads it as the separation of men and women in prayer. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the word «fitna» as leading astray, and note that no one can lead astray except one whom God has destined for the Fire. Al-Razi draws from this that the tempters have no effect without God's decree, while Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as affirming the angels' submission rather than any divine kinship. The readings converge on one point: the verse exposes the falsehood of those idolaters who had made promises and then rejected the message once it arrived.

This verse reports the words of the Meccan polytheists before the Prophet ﷺ was sent: if a Book like those of the earlier peoples, such as the Torah or the Gospel, or a warner like the one sent to the Jews and Christians, had come to them, they would have been sincere servants of God. The commentators agree that this was an empty wish, because when the Quran, the noblest of reminders, came to them, they rejected it, and so the threat that follows says they will soon know the consequences of their disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that the fa' in 'they disbelieved in it' implies an omitted clause, namely that the Book came and they rejected it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya stress the severity of this warning against their disbelief in their Lord and their rejection of the Messenger. Al-Qurtubi notes that these words were spoken when they were reproached for their ignorance, and he records the grammatical debate: for the Basrans, the 'in' is the lightened form of 'inna' and the lam marks the distinction, while for the Kufans 'in' means 'ma' and the lam means 'illa'. Al-Zamakhshari observes that they made these claims with insistence and earnestness, which makes their later denial all the more striking. In the context of the preceding verses, commentators say the angels are free of any claim of divine descent. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that 'the ranked ones' are the angels standing in rows for prayer or in their station before God, and 'the glorifiers' are those who pray or declare God free of what is unfitting for Him. Several hadiths are cited, notably the report from A'isha that every span of the heavens holds an angel standing or prostrate. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur hold that these details do not change the central meaning of the verse, which exposes the idolaters' claim and warns them.

This verse, the last of the polytheists' statements quoted in Surah as-Saffat, reports their earlier wish, made before the Prophet's mission, that if a Scripture like those given to the ancients had come to them, they would have been sincere servants of God. The commentators explain that the Scripture meant is one comparable to the Torah and the Gospel, and that the phrase means they would have devoted worship to God alone and would not have lied or disobeyed as others did. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi agree that this was said before the Prophet was sent, and that the particle fa in "then they disbelieved in it" introduces their later rejection of the Quran, described as the master of remembrances and the most excellent of books. Ibn Kathir sees the statement as a false wish, since the reminder came and they rejected it. Al-Tabari explains the desire as a Book or a prophet like those given to the Jews and Christians. Al-Qurtubi notes that the particle inna is a lightened form and that the lam marks the distinction from negation. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read the closing phrase, "so they will soon know", as a threat, and al-Jaza'iri says the outcome will be ruin if they do not repent. The commentators do not really disagree on the essential meaning. They differ on the reading of "al-mukhlasin": with a fatha on the lam it means those whom God has chosen, and with a kasra it means those who devoted their worship to God, two meanings that Ibn 'Uthaymin regards as inseparable.

This verse concerns the Meccan polytheists who, before the prophethood, wished that a scripture like those given to earlier peoples had come to them so they could devote their worship purely to God. When the Quran, the noblest of reminders, came to them, they rejected it, and God warns that they will soon learn the consequences of their disbelief. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, agree that the fa in 'fa-kafarū' is eloquent and implies an omitted clause: the reminder came, and they disbelieved in it. They agree that the warning is a pure threat. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the emphatic particles in their earlier claim make their later rejection all the more striking. Ibn 'Atiyya ties the rejection to envy. Regarding 'Our word has already preceded for Our messengers', al-Tabari understands it as God's decree that they will prevail through proof and support, while al-Mawardi gives two readings: victory by argument in this world and punishment in the next, or victory through faith or retribution. Al-Baghawi links it to the saying 'God has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail'. As for 'turn away from them for a time', al-Mawardi lists several views: the battle of Badr, the conquest of Mecca, death, or the Day of Resurrection. Scholars also differ on abrogation: Qatada holds the verse abrogated, while Mujahid holds it established. Overall, the verse threatens the disbelievers and reassures the believers of an ultimately victorious outcome.

This verse states that God had already decreed, before time, that His messengers would be given victory and that His army, meaning the believers who defend His religion, would prevail. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators understand this word as God's promise of support, citing the verse 'God has decreed: I and My messengers shall surely prevail.' Al-Tabari holds that this victory is achieved through proofs, while Ibn Kathir says it applies both in this world and in the hereafter. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that the victory covers both argument and warfare, and they note that the killing of some prophets or the defeat of some fighters does not contradict the promise, since the final outcome belongs to the messengers and their followers. Al-Hasan al-Basri reports that no prophet was ever defeated or killed in battle, whereas al-Qurtubi and others note that the assassination of some prophets does not contradict the promise. Al-Suddi and Mujahid take the victory to be by arguments, while Ibn Zayd and al-Kalbi take it to cover both this world and the next. The verse has several readings: most read 'kalimatuna' in the singular, al-Dahhak reads it in the plural, and Ibn Mas'ud reads 'ala' instead of 'li'. The verse then orders the Prophet to turn away from the polytheists for a while, and the commentators differ on what this 'while' refers to: the battle of Badr, the conquest of Mecca, death, or the Day of Resurrection. Some consider this ruling abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others hold it remains valid.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the warning to the disbelievers who rejected the Reminder that had come to them. It states that Allah had already decreed, before time, that His messengers would be helped and that His army, meaning the believers, would be the victors. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy read it as a promise of support and triumph, while al-Sa'di sees in it a great good news for everyone who belongs to Allah's army. Al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and al-Mawardi specify that this victory is first of all one of proofs and arguments, whereas Qatada and Ibn Zayd speak of victory through faith or through retribution. Al-Hasan states that no prophet was defeated in war or killed in battle, and Ibn 'Abbas says that if they are not helped in this world they will be helped in the next. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud point out that this promise is consistent with occasional setbacks, since the general pattern and the final outcome are victory. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the 'word' referred to is either the promise that Allah will prevail with His messengers or the verse itself. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as both a consolation for the Prophet and a message of success for the believers, with the emphasis on ultimate victory. These readings agree on the essential point: it is a promise of a favourable outcome, and they differ on the nature and timing of that victory.

This verse affirms that God decreed victory for His messengers and that His army, meaning the believers who defend His religion, will prevail, through the power of proof, through triumph in battle, and through success in the Hereafter. The commentators identify the "word" with the divine promise stated in "God has decreed: I and My messengers shall surely prevail," as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report.

Al-Tabari explains this victory as victory by arguments. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi extend it to both this world and the next, and al-Nasafi transmits from Ibn Abbas that whoever is not helped in this life will be helped in the afterlife. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Zamakhshari hold that the basic pattern of their affair is victory, even if setbacks or deaths occur in some battles. Al-Zamakhshari cites al-Hasan al-Basri, who said that no prophet was ever defeated in war or killed in it.

The commentators differ on the nature of this victory. Al-Sudi and al-Kalbi take it to mean victory by proofs in this world and punishment for the enemies in the next, while Qatada understands it as triumph through faith or through retribution. Al-Razi distinguishes victory by the strength of argument, victory by political dominance, and victory by lasting endurance. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as describing the usual outcome, without excluding rare defeats.

The commentators note that the verse consoles the Prophet and gives good news to the believers. Some read "word" as singular, while al-Dahhak read it as plural. Ali ibn Abi Talib specifies that God's army includes the angels in heaven and the fighters on earth.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the obstinate Quraysh and leave them for a time, while they await the punishment that will come upon them and that they will soon witness. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the Prophet is to bear their harm patiently and not fight them for now, and he is consoled with the assurance that final victory belongs to him and his followers. They differ on the meaning of this 'time'. Qatada and Ibn Abbas take it to be death, al-Suddi and Mujahid the day of Badr, Ibn Zayd the Day of Resurrection, and others the conquest of Mecca. Al-Tabari prefers al-Suddi's view because God threatens them with the punishment they had been demanding. Some hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others consider it still in force. As for 'and watch them', most take it to mean observe their outcome, while Tha'lab understood it as informing them now so that they will know it directly. The commentators agree that the mockers' eagerness for punishment is foolishness, and that the punishment descending upon them is a grim morning for those who were warned. The command to turn away is repeated for emphasis, and the surah closes by exalting God above what the polytheists attribute to Him, with peace upon the messengers and praise to God, Lord of the worlds.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the disbelievers for a time and then to watch, for they will soon see the punishment that will befall them. The commentators differ on the meaning of this "time". Qatada and Ibn Abbas take it to be death, al-Sudi and Mujahid the day of Badr, and Ibn Zayd the Day of Resurrection, while al-Naqqash reports the conquest of Mecca. Al-Tabari prefers al-Sudi's view, since the verse threatens the disbelievers with the punishment they were demanding. As for "and watch them", Qatada reads it as the moment when sight will no longer benefit them, Ibn Zayd as their seeing, in the Hereafter, what they neglected of God's command, and al-Zamakhshari as a consolation to the Prophet, the promised victory being as if before his eyes. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi see the verse as reinforcing the warning already given. All agree that "sawfa" signals a threat rather than distance, and that the disbelievers' urgency in demanding punishment shows their folly. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that some scholars regard the verse as abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others regard it as still in force. Ibn Ashur explains that turning away means ignoring their words rather than abandoning the call.

The commentators explain that this verse follows a warning to the disbelievers and puts a rebuking question to them: why do they seek to hasten the punishment they have been warned of? When it descends upon their courtyard, that is, in front of their homes, the morning will be evil for those who were warned and did not believe. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the sahah is the open space in front of a house, that the Arabs use the image of punishment landing in one's courtyard for whatever befalls a person, good or bad, and that the morning is mentioned because raids usually took place at dawn. The commentators agree that the command to turn away from them for a time is addressed to the Prophet, but they differ on how long that time is. Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Zajjaj say it means until death, al-Suddi and Mujahid, citing Ibn Abbas, say it means the day of Badr, Ibn Zayd says the Day of Resurrection, and al-Zamakhshari also mentions the conquest of Mecca. They also disagree on abrogation: Qatada and Muqatil ibn Hayyan hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others consider it still valid. On the phrase 'observe them, for they will soon see', Ibn Zayd takes it to mean they will see the consequences of their disbelief on the Day of Resurrection, al-Kalbi and Muqatil see it as the punishment at Badr, and some read it as both a promise to the Prophet and a threat to them. Most exegetes report that the disbelievers asked for the punishment mockingly, saying 'When will this promise be fulfilled?', and that such haste could show itself in speech or in conduct, meaning persistence in disobedience. Several cite the hadith of Anas about Khaybar to explain the phrase 'when we descend upon a people's courtyard', and al-Zamakhshari sees in the verse a striking image of an army falling suddenly upon a people who had been warned but did not prepare.

These verses state that God promised His messengers victory, and that His soldiers, the believers, will be the victors. He then commands His Prophet to turn away from the disbelievers for a set time and to await what will befall them. The commentators agree that the punishment descending upon their courtyard means their destruction, and that the verse depicts it as an army that surprises a people in their homes before they can prepare. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the word "morning" refers to the time of a raid, since the Arabs used to attack at dawn, so this is an allegorical image, which Ibn 'Ashur considers can be taken apart element by element.

The commentators differ on the "time" until which the Prophet is to turn away. Al-Sudi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean the battle of Badr; Qatada, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it to mean death; Ibn Zayd places it at the Day of Resurrection; al-Mawardi also reports the conquest of Mecca. Al-Tabari judges al-Sudi's view the closest to the apparent sense of the revelation. Some, such as Muqatil ibn Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya, consider the verse abrogated by the verse of fighting, while Mujahid holds it to be unabrogated.

The meaning of "and let them see" also varies: seeing what will happen to them according to Qatada and Ibn Zayd, waiting for their fate according to al-Tabari, or seeing their condition with the heart according to al-Mawardi. Commentators also note that the mockery of the disbelievers, who asked when this punishment would come, is the occasion of the verse's mention of their hastening. The hadith of Anas about Khaybar is cited by several exegetes to clarify the meaning of "the courtyard" and of "the morning."

God instructs His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to turn away from the polytheists among his people and leave them until the time God permits their destruction, and to watch, for they will see what befalls them. The commentators explain that this 'time' is either the hour of punishment or the moment the Prophet is commanded to fight them. Ibn Abbas took it to mean death, Mujahid the battle of Badr, Qatada death as well, Ibn Zayd the Day of Resurrection, and others the conquest of Mecca. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see the repetition of the verse as reinforcing what came before. Qatada and Muqatil ibn Hayyan held that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others considered it still valid. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the repetition offers consolation upon consolation and confirms the promise, and that leaving the verbs without an object implies that what the Prophet will see, and what they will see, cannot be fully described. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi report that some scholars took one 'time' to refer to this world and the other to the hereafter. The closing words, 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might', and what follows, are read by many as God being exalted above what the disbelievers attribute to Him. Al-Razi sees in this closing a summary of knowledge of God, of right conduct toward people, and of the state after death.

This verse tells the Prophet, peace be upon him, to turn away from the polytheists and leave them for a time, and to wait, for they will soon see what befalls them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that he should wait until God permits their punishment, and that seeing refers to witnessing the chastisement when it arrives. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note that the repetition serves as consolation and emphasis on the promise, and that the two verbs, left without an object, cover every kind of joy and harm. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'for a time': Ibn Abbas and Qatada say it means death, Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Tabari say the day of Badr, and Ibn Zayd says the Day of Resurrection, while Ibn Atiyya records further views. On abrogation, Qatada and Muqatil ibn Hayyan hold that the verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting, whereas al-Mawardi reports that others consider it still in force. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy also record these differences. Ibn Kathir cites the Khaybar report to illustrate the dawn attack, which al-Zamakhshari reads as a figurative image. Ibn Ashur suggests the second period may refer to the Prophet's lifetime or to the afterlife. The commentators do not choose between these readings, all of which point to strengthening the Prophet and warning the disbelievers.

The verse closes the surah by glorifying God, exalted above what the polytheists attribute to Him, namely offspring and partners. Its plain meaning is: glory be to your Lord, O Muhammad, Lord of might and power, far above what they describe. The commentators agree that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and that "al-'izza" means strength and victory. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that tasbih is the declaration that God is free of all that does not befit Him, and Qatada specifies that the description meant is falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan say that the Lord is joined to might because He alone possesses it, while al-Nasafi and others add that He is owner of all the might creatures enjoy. For "peace upon the messengers", Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as the messengers being safe from what was said about God, and al-Mawardi offers two readings: an honour they are given, or a guarantee of their safety from being killed. The verse ends with "praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds", which al-Tabari takes as exclusive praise for His blessings, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir take it as praise for the destruction of enemies and the support of the prophets, and al-Shawkani and Abu al-Su'ud as a general praise for all His favours. Several commentators relay traditions on the merit of reciting these verses at the end of prayer or of a gathering; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note their weakness, and no one settles the scholars' differences on this point.

God concludes Surat As-Saffat by declaring Himself free of what the idolaters attribute to Him, such as offspring and partners, for He is the Lord of might and glory. He then sends peace upon the messengers, meaning He affirms their safety and security, both from what their peoples did to them and from what they said about their Lord, and finally praises Himself for the blessings He bestows and the victory He gives to His prophets. Commentators explain that the peace here means greeting and honour, and also a promise of protection from harm and safety on the Great Day of Terror. By the messengers they mean the prophets who convey monotheism and the revealed laws, while some include the angels who carry out God's commands. They agree that what the messengers said about their Lord is free of all fault, which is why they are greeted with peace. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Ashur see the verse as a comprehensive summary of the sura's themes: glorifying God, honouring the messengers, and praising God for His favours. Ibn al-Qayyim understands the peace as a supplication that can come from God in the form of a commitment He makes to Himself. Reports from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Anas and others say the Prophet recited it at the end of his prayer or gathering, and that whoever recites it when leaving a gathering earns a full measure of reward, although most hadith scholars consider these chains weak. The commentators draw no specific legal ruling from the verse beyond the recommendation to recite it when closing a gathering.

This verse closes Surat as-Saffat by glorifying God, who is exalted above what the disbelievers attribute to Him, such as offspring and partners. He is the Lord of Might, who grants honour to whom He wills and humbles whom He wills. God then sends peace upon the messengers, since all they said of their Lord is free from any flaw, and He praises Himself for His blessings, for sending the prophets and for granting them victory over their enemies. The commentators present these lines as a summary that gathers the sūrah's main themes: the refutation of polytheist beliefs and the strengthening of the messengers.

The commentators agree that the praise can carry several meanings: thanking God for sending messengers as bringers of good news and warners, or for all His blessings upon creation, as al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir explain. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as praise for the destruction of the enemies and the victory of the prophets, while al-Qurtubi holds that all these meanings are intended together. Ibn Kathir links the glorification to the negation of imperfection and the praise to the affirmation of perfection.

On the phrase "Lord of Might", al-Mawardi offers two readings, "owner of might" or "Lord of everything that is mighty"; al-Zamakhshari explains the construction as an idiom of exclusivity, and Ibn 'Atiyya takes it to refer to the created might that men possess. As for the peace upon the messengers, al-Mawardi reads it either as an honour paid to them or as a declaration of their safety. Al-Tabari cites a report from Qatada about the greeting of peace to the messengers.

Several reports state that reciting these verses at the end of a gathering or after prayer brings a great reward, but Ibn Kathir and others point out the weakness of their chains of transmission, so these reports are not regarded as firmly established.
